The 10y breakeven sits at 1.62%, up 14bps over three weeks but down 11bps over a year, positioned mid-range within a 76bp 12-month band. Core PCE at 1.46% y/y has retraced from 1.41% and remains 54bp below the 2% target, but the 3-month annualised core rate of 1.99% signals real backbone underneath—not a soft disinflation story. Headline CPI momentum turned positive last month at +31bps and the 3-month annualised print sits at 54bps, a material rebound from the disinflationary phase but still well below normal. The core-minus-headline spread at 57bp is widening, pointing to goods disinflation losing momentum while services stickiness persists.

This is not slack, and the outright level sits 100bps above estimates of the natural rate. Wage pressure remains plausible but is not yet evident in the data. The financial conditions index has tightened sharply over the past month, moving from -0.27 to -0.35, now at the lower end of its 12-month range. This tightening acts as a modest brake on inflation dynamics and growth expectations.

The reconciliation here turns on expectations versus realised outcomes. Realised inflation (both headline and core annualised rates) has bounced back materially from lows, but expectations have not followed—they have actually drifted off recent highs. This is the classic "hot realised, anchored expectations" signature. The panel gives me no reason to flip expectations higher yet: the breakeven print is recent and modest, positioned in the middle of its band, and the 3-week rise is a bounce not a trend. The labour market is slack enough and financial conditions are tight enough that wage-driven persistence is not yet the marginal driver. Inflation expectations have drifted sideways and off their recent high, while realised inflation shows a mixed but moderately hot picture. The 10y breakeven sits at 1.62%, up 14bps over three weeks but down 11bps over a year, positioned mid-range within a 76bp 12-month band. The measurement panels reveal a bifurcated inflation picture that argues for narrowing 10y breakevens. Realized inflation is running hot: headline CPI year-over-year sits at 1.17% with a sharp +0.38% m/m outgoing, while the 3-month annualized headline rate of 2.27% and 3-month core of 1.99% both exceed recent trends. The momentum is decidedly upward—core PCE has moved from 1.19% to 1.46% in the last three months, and headline is near its 12-month high. This appears sticky, not transitory.

However, inflation expectations have already priced much of this in. The 10y breakeven stands at 1.71%, up 30 basis points over 63 days and 53 basis points above its 12-month low. It sits in the 70th percentile of its 12-month range, having captured the bulk of the realized inflation move. The expectations read is fresh and has been leading upward in tandem with realized inflation prints, not lagging. Meanwhile, the labor market is loosening modestly—unemployment has risen 30 basis points in 3 months and sits 110 basis points above the estimated natural rate, suggesting wage pressure is unlikely to sustain price momentum. The broader financial conditions backdrop is easing (NFCI at -0.39, near recent lows) and risk appetite has stabilized after earlier weakness.

The key tension is between hot near-term inflation data and already-elevated expectations that have priced it in, paired with a labor market that is cooling. The expectations measure has not lagged; it has moved with realized inflation and is now at a level that leaves less room for further widening if disinflation follows when labor tightness eases. Given that expectations are the marginal driver of breakevens and they have already adjusted significantly upward, the risk to the wedge is asymmetric toward narrowing as realizations moderate and expectations stay anchored around current levels. Near-term data will remain volatile (evidenced by the high spread between last month's 0.31% and the 3-month average of 0.19%), but the 12-month trend in expectations is negative (down 18bp), suggesting the anchor is holding despite recent noise.

Bet short T10YIE (shorter duration of inflation compensation).

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation has reaccelerated sharply in the near term. Headline 3-month annualised sits at 3.65%, with core PCE pushing to 1.57% year-over-year, up 10bp in the last three months. The monthly momentum picture is hotter still: headline at +0.28% m/m outgoing, with a 3-month average of +0.30%, suggesting momentum has re-established itself after the disinflationary summer. This is not a base-effect story—the year-over-year range has shifted: headline sits at 1.08%, in the 87th percentile of its 12-month distribution, well above the 0.01% floor. Core's distance from the 2% target has narrowed to -43bp, a meaningful tightening.

However, inflation expectations have compressed materially and moved the opposite direction. The 10-year breakeven has declined from 1.50% just weeks ago to 1.40% today, down 14bp in 21 days and 22bp in 63 days. Over a year it has fallen 47bp, now sitting at the 30th percentile of its 12-month distribution and 60bp below target. This is not a seasonal reversion; the trend is downward even as realised inflation accelerates.

The disconnect is the story. Realised inflation is running hot—3m annualised headline at 3.65% is sticky, and momentum is positive. But the market has decisively repriced inflation compensation lower. The labour panel shows unemployment ticking down to 4.90% from 5.20% three months ago, tightening by 40bp annually, with a Sahm gap of only 13bp. This should ordinarily support persistent inflation, yet expectations have not responded. The curve has flattened sharply: 2s10s slope is 91bp, down 78bp over 252 days, and sits near its recent lows. The 2s yield has fallen 33bp in three weeks, the 10s fallen 36bp.

The implication is that the market has moved from expecting persistent inflation to pricing in disinflationary momentum via either demand destruction, Fed credibility, or both. The 10-year breakeven is the market's final view on inflation compensation after all other considerations. The narrowness of that view—at the 30th percentile, deep below target, and falling as realised inflation rises—points to a belief that current hot prints are transient, or that the Fed's response will render them so. This is an expectations-anchored view, not a realised-inflation view. My read reconciles toward the expectations driver: the breakeven has collapsed and should narrow further if this dynamic persists.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation compensation has recently re-accelerated after a period of drift. The 10y breakeven sits at 1.73%, up 19bp over three weeks and 27bp over two months, closing in on its 12-month range high of 1.73%. This is a realised-inflation story: headline CPI growth has picked up sharply, with the latest print at 1.69% and a 3-month annualized rate of 2.76%, while core PCE has climbed to 1.78%, now 0.22pp from the 2% target. Momentum is unambiguously up — the last three headline prints average +0.24% m/m and exceed the trailing 12-month low by 1.25pp.

Inflation expectations, however, have not overshot. The 10y breakeven is still 0.27pp below target, and the recent rebound merely reflects a normalization from a depressed level rather than a blow-out shift in forward-looking anchoring. The curve slope, rising to 98bp over three weeks, suggests growth expectations are firming alongside inflation — not a panic-induced widening of nominal rates. Fed balance sheet continues to contract (−10.2bn over 13 weeks) and financial conditions remain loose at −0.37, consistent with steady policy accommodation, not restrictive tightening.

The labour market read is weak. Unemployment has drifted up to 4.90% and sits 90bp above the estimated natural rate, with a positive 3-month change offset by a 12-month decline. Wage pressure should be moderating. This tension — rising realised inflation but a labour market that does not support persistent wage-driven expectations — is the core of the reconciliation. Positioned asset managers and leveraged funds have sharply de-risked over the past month (asset manager z down from +0.95 to −0.07 std devs, lev funds down to −0.44), and positioning appears not to be anchoring expectations either.

The read is a near-term inflation tick that has correctly lifted expectations off the lows, but with limited runway. Without acceleration in either labour tightness or fresh Fed tightening, realised inflation should decelerate toward core, and the recent bump in compensation should fade as base effects roll off.
arbitrated.falsifier: Labour market suddenly re-tightens, or next CPI shows headline acceleration sustained above 2% annualized — either would force expectations higher.

risks.text: Curve slope rallying 15bp in three weeks signals growth repricing that could pull term premium; widening yields while breakeven steadies.
Asset manager and lev fund de-risking extreme (z-scores deeply negative); sharp reversal would hydraulically widen real yields and trap breakevens.
Fed balance sheet shrinking steadily; if tightening language emerges, forwards could reprice higher and anchor expectations above current 1.73%.
Breakeven at 12m range high with no fresh labour or expectation shock leaves room only for range-bound chop or reversal.

trade.rationale: Realised inflation up clearly, expectations up modestly off lows. Labour market slack widening should limit further compensation widening. Modest long position reflects near-term momentum but low conviction given positioning fragility and lack of fresh expectations catalyst.

why.inflation: Headline at 1.69%, 3m annualized 2.76%, momentum unambiguous. Latest three prints +0.24% m/m avg. Up clearly from 12m low.
why.inflation_expectations: Breakeven rebounded 27bp in two months but sits 27bp below target, at 12m high. Normalization, not anchor break.
why.labor_tightness: Unemployment at 4.90%, 90bp above natural rate. 3m change positive, 12m change negative. Slack is widening, wage fuel drying.

The near-term direction depends on whether this represents genuine expectations repricing or a temporary overshoot. Realised inflation shows a mixed picture: headline CPI has accelerated sharply (up 1.68% y/y, the highest in the 12-month window) and 3-month annualized headline stands at 2.49%, but this includes significant base effects and monthly volatility (+0.12% m/m most recently, after +0.23%). Core PCE has drifted up more persistently to 1.78% y/y and 1.77% annualized 3m, narrowing the gap to the Fed's 2% target to just 22bp. The labour market has tightened: unemployment hit 4.7%, down 40bp year-over-year and now sitting at the 12-month low, with a small positive Sahm gap (0.17pp) suggesting no recession warning. This tightness supports inflation persistence. However, the inflation-expectations anchor appears intact. Expectations at 1.94% are well-anchored to slightly-below-target, and the breakeven has risen in line with but not ahead of moves in nominal yields (10y up 51bp in 21 days, BE up 21bp). The recent steepening of the 2s10s curve (+26bp in 21d) reflects real rates, not expectations. Financial conditions remain accommodative (NFCI at -0.42, the tightest in 12 months but still loose), and the Fed balance sheet continues to shrink at a modest pace. Positioning shows asset managers have rotated sharply lower over the past month (currently at -0.59 std devs, well below the long-run mean), which could absorb further expectations repricing without necessarily triggering a widening of the wedge. The core inflation momentum is real and labour is tight, but expectations have not yet broken anchor. A stable or marginally higher breakeven over the near horizon is most likely, as realised inflation cools slightly from current high prints while expectations remain anchored near target. Any sustained break higher in expectations would require either a harder-to-disinflationary labour market or a larger surprise in core inflation persistence than the data currently suggest.

arbitrated.notes:
Current inflation has clearly risen over the year, with headline CPI now at 2.05% y/y and core PCE at 1.77% y/y. The momentum is substantial: headline is annualizing at 2.45% over three months, driven by material month-to-month readings averaging 0.20%. However, inflation expectations have remained remarkably stable and well-anchored. The 10-year breakeven sits at 1.95%, barely 0.01pp higher over the past 21 days, and just 0.39pp higher over 63 days despite the sharp rise in realized inflation. The expectations measure is positioned at the 95th percentile of its 12-month range, having recovered from 1.18% lows, but the gap between realized inflation momentum and expectations anchoring is the defining feature.

Labor tightness has loosened slightly; the unemployment rate now sits at 4.7%, down only 0.30pp over 12 months and currently at the low end of its recent range. The Sahm gap remains negligible at 0.07pp, indicating no recessionary signal. The labor market is tight relative to the Fed's natural rate estimate (0.70pp above), but not accelerating. This supports the inflation read without adding urgency to wage dynamics.

Financial conditions have tightened gradually. The NFCI is at −0.47, at its 52-week low (least accommodative), a 0.12-index move over 13 weeks. The 2s10s curve has flattened slightly over 21 days (−0.01pp to 1.25pp), though it is still elevated relative to the 12-month low of 0.76pp. These conditions are consistent with gradual monetary tightening but are not signaling acute stress.

The core read is that realized inflation has materially risen but expectations remain anchored. The stability of the 10-year breakeven, combined with recent volatility in positioning (asset managers at 0.91 std devs after a large 4-week swing) and moderating momentum in breadth, suggests the market is pricing in the near-term inflation surprise without repricing the inflation regime itself. The path for breakevens is constrained by anchored expectations acting as a ceiling, even as realized inflation runs hot. Over the horizon to the next CPI print, the expectation of a moderating headline momentum (the 3-month outgoing reading of −0.05% m/m is well below the recent 0.20% average) and persistent expectations anchoring should keep the 10-year breakeven range-bound to slightly narrower. The inflation compensation wedge is unlikely to widen materially if expectations remain protected.

Anchored expectations may reflect equilibrium at 2%, not a persistent ceiling; pass-through risk if labor data re-accelerates wage growth.

trade.rationale: Realized inflation hot but expectations anchored creates no clear breakeven directional edge over one month. Prefer to wait for clearer resolution of expectations durability.

arbitrated.notes: Realised inflation is running hot: headline CPI has jumped to 2.81% year-on-year, with the 3-month annualized rate at 3.31%, and core PCE at 1.86% is now 16bp above target. The month-on-month momentum remains positive at 0.31%, signalling persistence beyond base effects. However, inflation expectations remain anchored and remarkably stable. The 10-year breakeven has oscillated in a tight 2.00%–2.02% range over the last three observations, sitting just 2bp above the 2% target. Over 63 days the move has been modest at +13bp, and the level remains in the upper quartile of its 12-month range (92nd percentile), having already repriced up 63bp over the year. The disconnect between hot realised inflation and stable long-run expectations is the signature arbitration challenge here. The labour market supports inflation persistence: unemployment has tightened to 4.6%, moving further below the natural rate (now at 4.0% vs. 4.6% currently recorded), and the Sahm gap shows no recessionary signal yet. Tighter labour should support wage growth and inflation stick. Yet expectations pricing suggests the market sees this inflation as transitory or sees the Fed's policy response as sufficient to contain second-round effects. The Fed's balance sheet is essentially flat over 13 weeks (+0.07%) and 4 weeks (+15.9bn), down 21bn year-over-year. Financial conditions remain loose at 0.50 standard deviations below zero (at a 52-week low), and positioning in duration remains extremely long (asset managers at +2.07 std devs). The curve has flattened: the 2s10s slope is now 1.14pp, down 10bp over 63 days and at the bottom of a widening range. This flattening is consistent with expectations staying anchored even as realised inflation runs hot—the market is not demanding much additional term premium for inflation risk. On the balance of the evidence, breakevens appear correctly priced at current levels. The expectation of policy normalization and the anchored inflation expectations read outweigh the hot realised prints. However, the tightness of expectations around 2.0% alongside persistent labour tightness creates tail risk to the upside. If the market is forced to concede that inflation will remain above target for longer than currently embedded, breakevens would widen materially. The narrow range and long duration positioning leave little room to absorb a fresh upside surprise.

trade.rationale: Modest long breakevens. Realised inflation persistence and labour tightness support widening, but expectations are anchored and already repriced. The margin of safety is thin; curve flattening and extreme long positioning create tail risks to both directions.

arbitrated.notes: Inflation and expectations are diverging in a way that narrows the breakeven. Realized inflation is lifting: headline CPI year-on-year stands at 2.44% (up from 0.87% a year ago), and the 3-month annualized pace sits at 2.09%. Core PCE has moderated slightly to 1.68% but remains above the 2% target. The momentum is mixed—headline month-on-month turned negative at -0.05%, but this follows elevated readings and sits on a 3-month average of +0.17%, suggesting the base is genuinely hotter than it was. Labor tightness is clearly easing: unemployment has fallen to 4.40%, at the 12-month low and just 0.40 pp above natural rate. This tight labor market would normally support wage pressure and inflation persistence. However, expectations are anchored and actually drifting sideways to lower. The 10y breakeven sits at 1.97%, down 0.04 pp over the past three weeks and only 0.03 pp above its 2% target. Over 63 days it is up just 0.03 pp, and over the year it has climbed 0.32 pp from 1.34%, but the recent deceleration in that trend is notable. The range position at 0.85 shows breakevens are elevated within their 12-month band, but the latest level has not pushed higher—it has stalled and reversed slightly from 1.98% two observations ago. The Fed balance sheet is expanding modestly (up 11.6bn over four weeks, 18.2bn over thirteen) but remains 30bn below its 52-week high, so there is no sign of aggressive expansion supporting inflation expectations. The curve remains steeper than its 12-month low but has flattened 0.14 pp over 63 days and 0.04 pp over 21 days, which is consistent with a market that is pricing in both real rates holding and inflation compensation either flat or rolling over. This is the signature divergence: realized inflation hot, labor market tight, but market expectations stable and leveling. The cross-read is clear: expectations are not yet priced for sustained inflation from labor demand. The breakeven is narrow relative to what inflation momentum alone would suggest, and the direction of recent expectations flow is negative despite the macro setup that would normally support widening. This points to narrowing breakevens over the horizon as the recent modest lift in realizations fails to generate expectations momentum, and any disappointment in inflation prints or labor reports would reinforce the anchor.

Curve flattening alongside narrowing breakevens may not persist if labor market data surprise hot and steepen long end.

trade.rationale: Expectations are not yet responding to inflation momentum or tight labor. Breakevens have stalled and rolled over slightly despite the macro setup that should support them. The wedge narrows as realizations stay elevated but anchor expectations rather than lifting them further.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation expectations remain well-anchored near 1.92% despite a recent reacceleration in realized inflation that has brought headline CPI to 2.18% from 0.87% over the past year. The 10-year breakeven has drifted marginally higher over the past three weeks (+0.06pp) and sits at the upper bound of its 12-month range (0.78 range position), having risen 0.25pp over the full year. However, the recent 63-day decline of -0.16pp and the modest 21-day slip of -0.06pp suggest momentum has already begun to stall.

Realized inflation shows a more complex picture. Headline CPI has cooled sharply to 2.18% from a 2.81% peak, and the three-month annualized pace at 0.95% is well below the year-ago 2.44%. Core PCE has moderated similarly from 1.87% to 1.68%, although it remains 0.32pp above the Fed's 2% target. The month-over-month momentum is weak—headline came in at just 0.12% last month, down from 0.40% two months prior. This suggests base effects are dominant rather than underlying persistence.

Labor markets show tightness that has gradually eased. The unemployment rate sits at 4.40%, at the lower bound of its 12-month range, but the three-month change of -0.30pp and six-month change of -0.50pp both show moderation in the tightening pace. The Sahm gap remains negligible at 0.07pp, and the unemployment rate is only 0.40pp above the estimated natural rate—neither signaling imminent wage pressure acceleration.

The reconciliation: expectations are anchored and slowly drifting upward into technical resistance, while realized inflation is retreating visibly on softening momentum. Labor markets remain tight but are not accelerating further, which supports the view that inflation expectations will remain bounded. The wedge between expectations and realized inflation is set to narrow, not widen. The near-term direction of breakevens is toward consolidation and eventual modest narrowing as the realized inflation deceleration continues and expectations find a ceiling near the top of their range.

trade.rationale: Realized inflation cooling visibly (headline 2.18%, 3m annualized 0.95%) while expectations drift into range resistance at 1.92%. The wedge narrows as inflation disinflates and anchored expectations meet a ceiling. Position short breakevens over the one-month horizon.

The expectations analyst has not incorporated the actual deterioration in inflation dynamics or the material labour cooling into the forward-looking measure.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is cooling through base effects and moderating momentum. Headline CPI has fallen from 2.81% to 1.73% year-over-year over the last 13 months, a 108bp collapse. The 3-month annualised headline print is just 0.08%, showing negligible momentum. Core PCE has softened to 1.50% from a 1.87% peak, with 3-month annualised core at 1.16%. Month-on-month momentum is benign: the latest headline print is 0.03% m/m, and the 3-month average stands at only 0.01% m/m. This reflects a combination of base effects (the 12-month high of 2.81% rolls off progressively) and genuine disinflation in the data.

Inflation expectations, however, have ticked up slightly. The 10-year breakeven has moved to 1.82% from 1.76% at the start of the observation window, a 6bp rise over 21 days and a 38bp move from the 12-month low. The breakeven now sits 38bp above its 12-month low and in the upper half of its 12-month range (59th percentile). This suggests market participants are pricing in either more persistence or a smaller decline ahead than realised prints alone would warrant.

The labour market remains tight. Unemployment is at 4.30%, matching the 12-month low and sitting 30bp above the natural rate estimate. The 12-month trend is -50bp, but the momentum has moderated recently. The Sahm rule shows only a 3bp gap, implying labour tightness is present but not signalling imminent recession.

The disconnect between realised inflation falling sharply and expectations holding firm is the central tension. This is the signature anchoring case: the market believes current disinflation will prove temporary or that wage pressures will resurface, keeping long-term inflation compensation elevated. The Fed's balance sheet is essentially flat (-0.11% over 13 weeks, only -4.9bn in outflows), providing no active cooling impulse. The 2-10 curve slope has steepened to 96bp (from 88bp 63 days ago), which typically accompanies tighter financial conditions but also reflects a recalibration of growth and rate expectations rather than inflation-specific dynamics.

Given the sharp realised-inflation decline, the modest tightness in labour conditions, and stable expectations, the most likely path is for the 10-year breakeven to drift sideways to slightly lower as realised prints continue to release downside surprises relative to the expectations premium currently priced in. The market is overcautious on persistence risk, given how cleanly the disinflation has proceeded and how shallow momentum now sits.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation shows a tightening picture in the near term but with momentum fading. Headline CPI returned to +1.93% y/y last month after sliding from +2.81%, and the three-month annualized reads +1.95% — still above the longer-trend core picture of +1.43% y/y. The recent monthly print of +0.38% m/m is elevated, but the core-minus-headline gap of -0.49pp suggests base effects and energy volatility rather than broad-based pressure. Core PCE at +1.43% y/y, down 0.11pp over three months, sits 0.57pp below the 2% target. This is a realised picture that has cooled significantly from mid-year highs but is not yet in structural deflation.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, are entirely anchored and showing no urgency. The 10-year breakeven has oscillated between +1.74% and +1.76% over the last month — a range of just 2bp — and sits at +1.76% now, close to the midpoint of its 12-month range. Its change over 21 and 63 days is both -3bp, indicating zero drift. The market is pricing stable long-term inflation roughly 24bp below target, with zero signs of either acceleration or de-anchoring.

The disconnect here is the signature case: realised inflation is hot on the headline side and sticky on the core side despite the downtrend, yet expectations remain inert and centered at a below-target level. This argues strongly for expectations to anchor the wedge — the market is not pricing a belief that higher current inflation will persist, and there is no evidence in the expectations panel that it will reset higher.

Labour tightness presents a cross-read that tests persistence. The unemployment rate has drifted up slightly to +4.40% from recent lows, is up 0.40pp from its natural rate estimate, and the Sahm gap is near zero at +0.03pp. This is not a labour market signalling wage-push urgency. Over six and twelve months the trend is flat to slightly loose, supporting the view that current inflation pressure is not being reinforced by a tightening labour market holding back the disinflationary drift in expectations.

The Fed's balance sheet continues a slow contraction: assets down $10 billion over 52 weeks and currently $20.7 billion below their 12-month high. This is passive tightening that leans gently against inflation, not a driver of immediate repricing.

The reconciled read is that 10-year inflation compensation narrows over the horizon. Realised inflation will cool further as base effects and headline noise fade, bringing both headline and core closer to the target band. Anchored expectations will not reset higher — they have no reason to, given weak labour dynamics and the inflation trend. The wedge compresses as realised inflation gravitates down toward the expected level already priced in.

Realised inflation shows a classic two-tier picture: headline has reaccelerated sharply with a 3.77% annualized 3-month read and a 54bp jump over the past quarter, driven by a 51bp month-on-month move that overshot the 23bp outgoing baseline. Core PCE has decelerated instead, down 11bp over the same window to 1.43%, now 57bp below target. This core-headline divergence points to base effects and energy volatility, not persistent breadth. The labour market remains tight but has stabilized: unemployment is at its 12-month low of 4.3%, and while the 3-month change is flat at zero, the 6-month and 12-month trends show cumulative tightness. Wage dynamics should tighten further if labour supply does not ease, but the unemployment rate itself is not accelerating now.

Inflation expectations anchor sharply. The 10y breakeven at 1.84% sits 16bp below the 2% target and has gained only 8bp over the past 21 days, 11bp over 63 days, and 32bp over the past year. The range position of 0.56 shows the BE is in the upper-middle of its 12-month band. Breakevens have drifted sideways over recent weeks despite the headline reacceleration, suggesting the market is pricing this as transient rather than structural.

The tension is clear: realised headline inflation has jumped, but expectations remain anchored and have not re-priced in response. This is the signature case where inflation persistence is questioned by what the expectations market is willing to price. Core inflation is slowing, which is the rate-relevant signal; headline noise should not override that. The two-month chart on headline momentum does show an elevated 4-week outgoing read, but this remains consistent with base effects and energy noise rather than a shift in the persistent component.

On balance, the reconciliation leans toward expectations staying anchored and the headline reacceleration fading back toward core. If that happens, 10y breakevens compress. The risk is if core stabilizes rather than continuing to drift lower, or if labour tightness forces wages higher in a way the expectations market has not yet priced. But the current panel does not show that yet.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is accelerating on a 3-month annualized basis, with headline CPI rising to 3.47% annualized and monthly momentum picking back up to +0.27% m/m. The 3-month core print at 1.92% annualized is less concerning but shows a tick from the lows, and core is running above its 12-month low. However, inflation expectations have softened meaningfully on the 21-day horizon (down 0.02pp to 1.86%), sitting 0.14pp below the 2% target and near the bottom of its recent range at 1.66% low. The 63-day and 252-day slopes on breakevens are flatter, with the 63-day at +0.10pp showing only modest recovery.

The labour market remains tight but has cooled. The unemployment rate is at a 12-month low of 4.20%, but has been range-bound recently and the 3-month/6-month changes are -0.20pp, indicating a plateau rather than continued deterioration. The Sahm gap sits at a benign +0.03pp and the rate sits 20bps above the estimated natural rate, suggesting slack is present but not dramatic.

The Fed's balance sheet is contracting steadily. Year-to-date assets are down 15.2bn, and the 13-week change of -13.2bn shows the contraction is ongoing, though not accelerating. The curve has flattened significantly over 12 months (down 57bps in slope), and currently sits at 64bps, near the middle of its recent range but at the lower end of a year-wide band.

The tension here is classic: hot realized inflation being offset by softening expectations. On the expectations side, the 21-day move is the most staleness-critical signal, and it shows clear retreat. The fact that core expectations are not riding on an elevated base but instead cooling into a post-inflation-shock regime suggests the market is pricing in some combination of demand moderation and policy restraint. The realized prints are eye-catching but still well within post-pandemic normal, and the 3-month core at 1.92% annualized is not a persistence signal so much as a reversion from deep trough lows. The labour tightness is real but no longer tightening, which removes a key feedback loop into wages and persistence.

Given that expectations are the dominant driver of the breakeven wedge over the medium term, and the recent 21-day move is materially lower while the longer-term floor (12-month low of 1.66%) is also being tested, the case is for a modest narrowing of 10y breakevens from here. The realized acceleration is noise around a cooling trend; the expectations reset is the signal.

arbitrated.notes:
The panel reveals a divergence between realised inflation and inflation expectations that is decisive for the 10y breakeven read. Realised inflation shows mixed momentum: headline has stabilised around 2.1–2.2% y/y with monthly prints bouncing (0.21% last month, down from 0.27% the month before), while core PCE has edged higher to 1.58% y/y, moving away from the recent low of 1.43%. The 3-month annualised measures—headline at 2.24%, core at 1.78%—suggest underlying stickiness, though core remains well below the 2% target. Labour tightness is genuinely tightening: unemployment has fallen to 4.1%, the lowest in the 12-month window, with a 60bp decline over the year. This is the material support for wage persistence and thus inflation persistence.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, have shown only modest movement. The 10y breakeven has climbed 12bp over three weeks and 9bp over two months, but is flat (1bp) over a full year, sitting at 1.96%—just 4bp below the 2% target and bang in the middle of recent trading. The range-position metric at 0.71 shows the breakeven is in the upper half of its 12-month band, but the band itself is only 42bp wide, indicating tight anchoring.

This is the signature case the instructions flag: realised inflation showing persistence through labour tightness, but expectations remaining anchored. The labour analyst's informed cross-read validates that tightness is real and durable. The recent 3-week move in breakevens (+12bp) is shallow relative to the momentum in underlying inflation, and the 21-day slope steepener (-8bp in 2s10s) suggests the near-term inflation surprise is being priced mostly into the front curve, not the long end.

The reconciliation: inflation will likely remain sticky in the near term (3–6 months) because labour is tight and core is edging higher. But long-dated expectations are already properly anchored at 2%, and market pricing reflects that. The 10y breakeven will narrow over the meeting horizon because the recent real-inflation surprise is exhausting, because longer-dated inflation expectations will stay moored despite labour tightness, and because the curve flattening already reflects this repricing of long-duration real rates rather than expectations. The trade is a narrowing of the inflation wedge.

{"notes": "Inflation compensation is moving higher across both near-term and longer-horizon measures, driven by a pickup in realised inflation that is beginning to push expectations, though expectations remain well-anchored relative to the heat in the data. Headline CPI has rebounded sharply: the most recent print stands at 2.15% y/y with a 3.43% m/m annualized momentum that is well above the recent outgoing baseline, and the recent three-month annualized print of 3.67% signals material near-term pressure. Core PCE has ticked up to 1.63% y/y from recent lows, adding 0.09pp over the last three months. This is the realised-inflation driver: both components are now reversing earlier disinflationary trends and moving back toward target.

The expectations response so far is measured. Ten-year breakevens have moved from 2.05% to 2.11% over the last three weeks, a 6bp rise. The move is modest in absolute terms—only 4bp of year-on-year change—and breakevens remain at the high end of their 12-month range. The labour market is also shifting. Unemployment has fallen to 4.0%, tightening 0.70pp over a year and now at the bottom of the 12-month range, suggesting wage pressure may begin to feed inflation expectations if current tightness persists.

The key tension is timing and persistence. The recent inflation surprise is in headline, where energy and base effects have played a role in the rebound. The 3.67% three-month annualized number includes a very recent sharp monthly jump (+0.43% in the latest month) that may not be fully structural. Core PCE is firming but still sits only 0.37pp above the 2% target, leaving room for market to treat the current pulse as transitory rather than a sustained regime shift. Breakevens have risen, but the pace of rise has been gentle—the 63-day change of +24bp is more notable than the 21-day +15bp, suggesting the repricing has been gradual and partial. This is consistent with expectations remaining anchored even as realised inflation flexes.

Unemployment has fallen to 4.0%, tightening 0.70pp over a year and now at the bottom of the 12-month range, suggesting wage pressure may begin to feed inflation expectations if current tightness persists.

Core PCE is firming but still sits only 0.37pp above the 2% target, leaving room for market to treat the current pulse as transitory rather than a sustained regime shift. arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation shows a modest rise, with headline CPI reaching 2.33% (top of its 12-month range) and core PCE at 1.91% (a recent high). The 3-month annualised rates are firm at 2.89% headline and 2.96% core, suggesting momentum has reaccelerated slightly after a period of moderation. Month-on-month prints have been volatile but non-trivial; the outgoing momenta support a near-term tick higher in year-on-year readings. Headline is 0.69 pp above its 12-month low and sits at the top of its recent band.

Inflation expectations, however, show clear anchoring. The 10y breakeven has compressed 7 basis points over the past three weeks and sits at 2.05%, only 5 basis points above the Fed's target. Over the full year, it has drifted modestly higher (8 bp) but remains well-contained within a 48 bp range, and positioning within that range is at the 81st percentile—near the top but not at extremes. The breakeven has not responded to the recent inflation pickup; the disconnect is the key signal here.

Labour tightness shows the unemployment rate at 4.0%, near its 12-month floor, but the 3-month and 6-month trends are actually loosening (down only 0.10 pp and 0.30 pp respectively over those horizons). The Sahm gap is negligible at 3 basis points, and the level sits exactly at the estimated natural rate. This suggests labour market tightness is no longer a material driver of wage pressure or inflation persistence—the data does not support a "hot" labour backdrop pushing expectations higher.

The reconciliation is straightforward: realised inflation has ticked up modestly, but expectations remain firmly anchored and have actually retracted slightly. Labour tightness is not acute. The absence of any upward response in breakevens to the recent inflation bump is the signature case for anchored expectations trumping a temporary realised-inflation pulse. Over the month ahead, barring a significant shock to the inflation prints or labour data, breakevens should either remain stable or continue to drift down modestly as the market continues to price in disinflation as base effects and any residual momentum fade.

trade.rationale: Inflation expectations are anchored and retracting despite a modest realised-inflation uptick; labour is not tight. Breakevens narrow over the horizon as market reprices the transience of the recent print bump and anchoring holds. Moderate conviction reflects near-term momentum volatility.

Realised inflation is now pushing higher across both headline and core measures, with headline CPI at 2.47% y/y and core PCE at 1.91%, both at the top of their 12-month ranges. Recent momentum is strong: the 3-month annualized core pace sits at 2.96%, headline at 2.22%, and this month's headline MoM was +0.26% with a positive surprise vs. the outgoing read. The labour market remains tight at exactly its 12-month low of 4.00% unemployment, with zero slackness on most metrics. This combination—hot realised inflation paired with a tight labour market—points to persistent upside pressure.

Inflation expectations, however, have been remarkably stable. The 10y breakeven sits at 2.17%, anchored within a tight range near its 12-month high. The most recent 21-day change is +0.12pp and the 63-day is +0.08pp—both modest gains that lag the acceleration in realised inflation. Expectations have drifted only +0.26pp over a full year, and at 2.17% they rest 0.17pp above the 2.0% target but show no signs of de-anchoring. The breakeven is at the 98th percentile of its 12-month distribution, suggesting it has already priced in available tightness.

The signature case for breakeven widening is when realised inflation accelerates while expectations remain anchored. Here, realised momentum has picked up visibly—both core and headline are now in their upper ranges and showing positive momentum—but expectations have barely budged. This is typically the regime where market participants gradually price in persistence.

However, two important caveats temper this read. First, the financial conditions panel shows mild tightening over the past month (NFCI at -0.53, up 0.09pp on the quarter), which could slow the real economy and cap inflation persistence. Second, and more material, the 2s10s slope has compressed from 0.54pp to 0.46pp over 21 days, and sits at only the 8th percentile of its 12-month range. A compressed, near-flat curve late in a cycle often signals market expectations of disinflation and policy pivot—not re-anchoring of higher inflation.

The labour read is genuinely tight, with no 12-month improvement. If wage pressure were feeding into expectations, we would see breakeven creep. That it has not, despite tight labour and hot core CPI, suggests expectations managers believe either (a) policy will cool demand sufficiently, or (b) this inflation bump is transitory. The curve flattening leans toward (a).

On balance, realised inflation is clearly higher and labour remains tight, but expectations are stable and the curve is flattening. Over a month-ahead horizon, the most likely path is a modest widening of the inflation wedge as realised momentum persists and begins to pull expectations slightly higher, but any move will be constrained by curve-flattening signals and financial conditions tightening. This is a mild widening, not a breakout.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has peaked and is rolling over on both the headline and momentum fronts. Headline CPI year-over-year has fallen from 2.85% to 2.33%, a material decline, with three-month annualized momentum at just 1.87% and the current month-over-month print at 0.21%. Core PCE has retreated to 1.90% from a 2.00% high, undershooting the Fed's 2% target slightly. The disinflation momentum is clear and is being driven by both base effects winding down and underlying price pressures that have moderated substantially.

Labor tightness is tightening further, however. The unemployment rate sits at 3.70%, down from 4.30% twelve months ago and 3.80% three months ago. The labour market is at the tighter end of the recent range and appears to be strengthening. This is the inflation risk to monitor: sustained wage pressure in a tight labour market could prevent the disinflation from embedding itself into expectations.

Inflation expectations themselves remain remarkably well-anchored despite the inflation print noise. The 10-year breakeven trades at 2.14%, only 0.02pp higher over the last three weeks and 0.03pp over the last two months. The measure is sitting near its midpoint of the 12-month range (0.89 position), 0.14pp above target, and shows no sign of ratcheting up or down. Expectations have been sticky and stable, even as realised inflation has moved around. This is the signature of an expectations anchor holding.

The reconciliation is straightforward: realised inflation is falling and momentum is shallow, labour tightness is real but not yet translating into wage acceleration that the data would reflect, and expectations are anchored and stable. Over a one-month horizon to the next CPI release, headline inflation is likely to stabilise near current levels or soften further, and there is no reason to expect expectations to widen the 10y breakeven. The asymmetry between a weakening realised inflation picture and a labour tightness that has not yet broken through to wage-driven disinflation risks favours a narrowing wedge rather than widening, or most likely, continued stability. The expectation anchor is the dominant signal.

Core PCE has turned sticky near 1.87% y/y with the recent three-month annualized rate just 1.42%, which undershoots the 1.87% current level, but the trend has been choppy rather than decisively disinflating. The realized inflation path now sits mid-range on the 12-month scale (0.50 position), with the headline print 36 bp above its 12-month low.

Breakeven inflation expectations, however, have deteriorated markedly. The 10y breakeven has compressed to 2.05%, down nine basis points over the last three weeks and eight basis points over the last nine weeks. This represents a clear and sustained downward move that places it near the lower end of its 12-month range (0.63 position), now 22 bp above the 12-month low of 1.83% but well below recent highs. The breakdown is stale by one month's standard—we are looking at month-end data—but the directional signal is unambiguous: expectations have detached downward from the modest recent uptick in realized inflation.

Labor remains tight at 3.80% unemployment, roughly 0.20 pp below the estimated natural rate and unchanged over the last three months. This delivers no fresh signal of labor loosening and continues to underpin wage/inflation persistence risks. However, with no current wage or earnings acceleration explicitly flagged in this month's panel, the labor tightness alone cannot override the expectations deterioration.

The resolution here is straightforward: realized inflation is bumpy-sideways with a slight upward tilt, but inflation expectations are breaking lower in a way that substantially outweighs that signal. The wedge should narrow over the horizon because the expectations channel is pulling down the breakeven more decisively than realizations are pulling it up. This is the signature case where the two diverge—actual inflation sticky, expectations anchoring—and the rule is to resolve toward the expectations driver.
arbitrated.falsifier: Breakeven inflation rebounds sharply (>10bp) on the next print, or inflation accelerates decisively above 3.0% headline without expectations following.

risks.text: Leveraged funds have whipsawed from -1.79 to +1.08 std devs; a crowded short in breakevens could snap back.
Slope at 28bp, near 12m low; if it steepens sharply, real expectations could tighten and lift breakevens.
Persistent labor tightness (3.80% unrate) could force Fed to hold higher longer, supporting inflation compensation.
10y yields up 78bp in 12m; breakeven compression could reverse if nominal yields roll over without inflation falling.

trade.rationale: Breakeven expectations are breaking decisively lower while realizations remain stuck sideways-to-up. The wedge narrows as expectations pull down faster than inflation lifts it. Position short 10y inflation compensation over the month horizon.

why.inflation: Headline CPI re-accelerated to 2.49%; m/m momentum at 0.23% slightly above 3m average. But core PCE soft; sideways, not clearly rising.
why.inflation_expectations: 10y BE down 9bp in 3w, 8bp in 9w. Now at 2.05%, near 12m low. Clear downward break from recent realizations.
why.labor_tightness: Unemployment at 3.80%, 0.20pp below natural rate; flat 3m. Tight but no fresh signal of widening or tightening.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has cooled sharply from recent peaks, with headline CPI at 2.15% YoY (down 0.50pp over three months) and core PCE at 1.87% YoY. The most recent month shows a sharp deflationary print (headline -0.07% m/m), with the 3-month annualized trajectory at just 1.49%, well below the 2.85% peak seen in the cycle. This represents a genuine disinflation, not base effects alone.

Inflation expectations, however, have stabilized and begun to drift upward. The 10y breakeven stands at 1.97%, down only 8bp over three weeks but up 13bp year-to-date, and positioned in the middle-to-upper half of its 12-month range (38th percentile). Expectations are now sitting just 3bp below the Fed's 2% target, having recovered from the 1.84% low seen roughly a year ago.

The labour market shows no tightening pressure that would sustain inflation. The unemployment rate is stable at 3.8%, flat over three and six months, with only modest tightening of 40bp over twelve months and no forward pressure evident. The Sahm gap is negligible at 7bp, and slack remains: unemployment sits 20bp below the estimated natural rate but this reflects a modest buffer rather than acute tightness.

Financial conditions have tightened significantly. Fed assets have contracted by $341bn over the past year (52-week change), and the 2s10s slope has flattened by 38bp year-over-year, now sitting at just 21bp—the lowest in the range and near the critical zone where curve inversion fears resurface. The NFCI index has improved to -0.48 from -0.62 a year ago, but this still reflects accommodative conditions overall.

The critical divergence here is between realised disinflation and expectations anchoring. Realised inflation is falling clearly; expectations are holding or drifting higher. This is the textbook signature case—resolve toward expectations, not a split read. With labour showing no persistence mechanism and financial conditions actually tightening rather than supporting inflation through credit expansion, the floor under inflation compensation should remain anchored near current levels. Near-term realised inflation weakness is unlikely to drive expectations lower, as it appears structural (transportation, energy) rather than cyclical. The Fed's messaging on data-dependence and the lack of demand pressure both support stable-to-slightly-elevated expectations rather than a re-anchoring downward.

Over the one-month-ahead horizon, 10y breakevens are more likely to remain range-bound or drift slightly wider rather than narrow further. The combination of falling realised inflation with stable expectations leaves limited room for compression, and the shift from disinflation momentum to stabilization is already being priced in.

Wage pressure is not visible in the inflation reads, and the labour market's slight softening argues against expectations ratcheting up from labour demand side.

Financial conditions have tightened modestly (NFCI at -0.48, up 0.08 from 13 weeks ago), consistent with slower growth and lower rate expectations rather than inflation support.

The reconciliation is clear: the inflation wedge should narrow. Realised inflation is falling toward target, expectations remain anchored despite a brief recent firmness, and labour is loosening not tightening. The 10y breakeven should compress as the realised-inflation anchor gains weight over the forward-looking wedge.

Realised inflation shows a mixed picture. Headline CPI year-over-year has risen to 1.88% from 1.49% three months prior, but core PCE has fallen sharply to 1.62% from 2.04% over the same period. The inflation panel does not present a clear uptrend—rather, a bounce in headline layered over a core disinflationary trend. This is the signature case: realised inflation showing heat while core expectations remain anchored.

Expectations are the key here. The 10y breakeven has risen modestly to 1.88% from a recent low of 1.83%, but remains 0.20pp below its 52-week high and sits 0.12pp below the 2% target. The recent 21-day change of -0.07pp and 63-day change of +0.14pp suggest a range-bound, tentatively stable state rather than a widening wedge. The breakeven is in the upper half of its 12-month range (0.40 quantile), but the uptrend is shallow and interrupted.

Labour tightness shows the unemployment rate steady at 3.80%, with a Sahm gap of only +0.17pp and the rate sitting 0.20pp below the estimated natural rate. Over 12 months, unemployment has tightened by 0.20pp. The 3-month trend is slightly easier (-0.10pp), but this is noise around an equilibrium near the lower end of the neutral range. Labour is tight but not accelerating tighter, which ordinarily would support persistence of wage-driven inflation. However, the gap between core and headline inflation (-0.27pp) suggests that core disinflation is dominating, not wage spillovers.

The most parsimonious reading: headline inflation is bouncing on base effects and transitory momentum (the 0.38% m/m print is an outlier), while expectations remain anchored and core inflation continues to drift lower. The labour market is snug but not tightening further. Taken together, this tilts toward expectations remaining stable or even loosening modestly as the transitory headline bounce fades and realised core disinflation persists. Breakeven inflation compensation appears likely to narrow over the next month. The inflation panel shows a headline mix with near-term momentum—three-month annualized headline is 4.30% and recent mom prints are elevated at +0.38%—yet core PCE has decelerated sharply (1.62% y/y, down 0.42pp in three months). The divergence between hot headline momentum and core cooling signals base-effect and energy transience rather than persistent demand-driven inflation, a reading reinforced by labor market loosening.

Unemployment has drifted lower recently (3.70% last), but the three-month average sits at 3.77% with minimal tightness signals; the Sahm gap is near zero and the rate sits only at the 12-month low edge. This loose labour read undermines any case for wage-driven persistence pushing expectations higher. The labor tightness panel lacks conviction either direction given the chop, but leans toward cooling rather than tightening pressure.

Inflation expectations themselves show near-perfect stasis: breakeven 10y sits at 1.95%, just 0.07pp above the 21-day change and down 0.22pp over the year. The range position at 0.54 indicates mid-range anchoring. Expectations have not yet repriced to the recent headline bump; they remain well-behaved and 0.05pp below the 2% target. Financial conditions remain accommodative (NFCI at -0.61, at 12-month low), which typically supports stable expectations.

The critical asymmetry: realised headline inflation shows near-term upside momentum while expectations sit dormant. This is the signature "hot prints, anchored expectations" setup. In such cases, the expectations read dominates—markets are not pricing wider breakevens, and the labour softness provides no mechanism to drive them there. The Fed's messaging and term premium compression (10y down 0.52pp over 12m) reinforce expectation anchoring.

Over the next month, with core already cooling and headline base effects likely to roll off, realised inflation should decelerate toward trend while expectations remain stuck. This points to narrowing of the inflation compensation wedge rather than widening.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is losing momentum despite a recent uptick in headline momentum. The three-month annualised headline CPI sits at 3.16%, well above the core 1.59%, but this is driven by volatile energy and food components—note the outgoing mom (0.09%) sits well below the recent 3m average of 0.26%. Core PCE, the Fed's preferred measure, has been drifting lower: the 3m change is -0.18pp, with the current 1.56% y/y sitting 0.44pp below the 2% target. The 12-month range for core is narrow and compressed toward the low end, suggesting base effects are normalizing and underlying momentum is soft.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, have deteriorated materially. The 10y breakeven stands at 1.74%, down 0.35pp over the past year and 0.22pp over the past two months. It sits 0.26pp below the 2% target and near the 12-month low of 1.68%. The range position is very low (0.12), indicating expectations are anchored at the soft end of recent trading. This is precisely the signature case: realised inflation hot-ish on headline prints while expectations stay anchored—indeed, they've drifted lower despite the recent headline moves.

The labour market is tightening at the margin: unemployment has fallen to 3.6%, down 0.20pp over the year and now at the 12-month low. Sahm gap is only 0.10pp, showing limited slack. However, the tightness here is not translating into broader wage or inflation-expectations pressures. Core PCE momentum remains subdued and expectations have declined.

The Fed's balance sheet continues shrinking, down 3.1% over 13 weeks and nearly 477B over the past year, moving further below the 12-month high. This is deflationary mechanical support—less liquidity in the system. Financial conditions have eased slightly (NFCI at -0.58, very close to the 52-week low of -0.61), but remain accommodative. The curve slope at 0.19pp is historically flat but stable over recent weeks.

The critical read: core inflation is soft and decelerating; headline is propped up by transitory base effects and energy volatility. Expectations have anchored downward and show no sign of rising despite tight labour markets. This gap between labour tightness and inflation-expectations quiescence is the crux. Wage growth has not yet proven sufficient to ratchet expectations higher, and the lagged disinflationary effects of higher rates are still working through. Breakevens should remain range-bound to slightly lower over the near horizon, as the realised inflation impulse fades while expectations stay moored.

arbitrated.notes:
The inflation data shows core PCE slightly above target at 1.75% y/y, with the 3-month annualized pace at 1.66%, while headline sits at 1.74%. The inflation trajectory has been volatile but is not accelerating—headline is down 0.06pp over three months and core up only 0.18pp, both modest moves. Crucially, the monthly momentum is deteriorating: the most recent headline mom print is 0.09% m/m, well below the 0.21% outgoing, and the 3-month average is only 0.10% m/m. This suggests base effects are rolling off without fresh price pressure underneath.

Breakevens, however, are remarkably compressed and stuck. The 10y breakeven sits at 1.55%, a full 45bp below the 2% target, and has fallen 15bp over the past three weeks and 56bp over twelve months. Critically, the recent action is flat to down: the latest observation is 1.55% after a pop to 1.59%, showing no persistence. The breakeven panel gives no sign of fresh anchor drift or expectations reset—it is pinned near the 12-month low with near-zero buffer above it.

Labor markets remain tight but show a slight easing trend. The unemployment rate is 3.60%, down 20bp from a year ago and anchored at the 12-month low. Three-month change is flat, but six- and twelve-month trends are deflationary for wage pressure. The Sahm gap is minimal at 3bp, and the natural rate buffer is still 40bp—suggesting some slack exists, though not dramatically.

The Fed balance sheet has contracted sharply over one year (−459B, −10.8% of assets), which constrains QE tail risk and limits duration renewal. This tightens financial conditions in the medium term, a headwind for reflation pricing.

Reconciling these reads: realised inflation is soft and slowing, with weak monthly momentum. Expectations are deeply anchored—undershooting target and immobile. The labour market is tight but not accelerating tightness. The disagreement between the two does not support widening breakevens; instead, it reinforces that expectations are sticky low. The Fed's balance-sheet contraction removes a potential source of duration demand and inflation-hedge demand going forward.

Over the horizon, the base case is for breakevens to remain range-bound to slightly lower. Inflation momentum is insufficient to push expectations higher, and the expectations anchor itself is the governing constraint. A flare-up in monthly prints or fresh labour market tightness could shift this, but the data do not point there now.

trade.rationale: Inflation is soft, expectations are anchored far below target and immobile, labour markets are tight but not tightening. No clear directional edge; risk/reward is balanced. Flat is the honest read.

Inflation compensation is contracting on the back of a sharp, multi-month deterioration in realized inflation expectations. The 10y breakeven has fallen 52bp over a year and 16bp over three months, tracking lower even as headline realized inflation has stabilized around 1.7–1.8% y/y. The near-term read is unambiguously downward: breakevens sit at 1.54%, near the bottom of the 12-month range (1.48–2.07%), and have drifted down 2bp in the past three weeks despite a 4bp tick higher in the nominal 10y yield.

The realized inflation picture is mixed but leans benign. Headline CPI stands at 1.73% y/y, down from 2.49% a year ago, with a modest recent uptick in monthly momentum (0.28% m/m, annualizing to 2.13% over three months). Core PCE at 1.62% y/y is below target but has stabilized after a disinflationary spell. The gap between core and headline has narrowed to –11bp, suggesting no dramatic energy spike. Crucially, the momentum data is noisy—the 3-month headline annualized rate masks a volatile month-to-month pattern (ranging from –0.08% to +0.38% in the recent window)—so the true underlying pace remains ambiguous.

Labour tightness has eased modestly. The unemployment rate has drifted down to 3.6% and sits 40bp below the estimated natural rate, but the 3-month change is only –10bp and the 12-month span is equally flat at –20bp. The Sahm rule remains benign at +7bp. This suggests neither a significant tightness shock nor imminent loosening. The labour market remains supporting wage pressure, but not accelerating it.

The disconnect is between a realised-inflation read that is neither strongly disinflating nor persistently hot, and a breakeven market that has priced in disinflationary drift. The expectations curve is being set by the same multi-month slowdown observed in realized measures, but the expectations read has overshot: breakevens are now at the bottom decile of their year-long distribution and have de-anchored further despite stable underlying inflation. This reversion to no-view bias—treating the stale expectations read as the marginal driver—is justified because expectations are the determinant of the inflation wedge. A stable labour market and mixed near-term inflation momentum offer little reason to expect further rapid compression in inflation compensation beyond what has already priced in.

The directional risk is asymmetric: upside risk to inflation from a tighter labour market than the measures suggest, or a surprise in energy/commodity prices, would widen breakevens sharply from these depressed levels. Downside risk—a sharp economic slowdown or a policy shock—is already partially reflected in the low nominal yields and narrow curve slope.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation readings show conflicting momentum. Headline CPI sits at 2.34% y/y after a recent spike to 2.60%, with the 3-month annualized pace elevated at 2.14%. The latest monthly print came in soft at 0.05% m/m, but the outgoing 0.38% m/m is still above the 3-month average of 0.18%, suggesting transient momentum rather than trend. Core PCE has edged up slightly to 1.59% after drifting lower, though the 3-month annualized at 1.85% sits meaningfully above the y/y level, pointing to acceleration in the core. The span between headline and core has widened to -0.75pp, unusual in a tightening regime.

Against this, breakeven inflation expectations have compressed sharply. The 10y breakeven has fallen to 1.41%—the absolute 12-month low, having fallen 23bp in three weeks and 51bp over a year. The positioning is stark: the measure now sits at the bottom of its 12-month distribution (range position 0.00). This anchoring of expectations amid a hot inflation print is the key wedge. It suggests either that markets are discounting near-term inflation as transient, or that real-rate repricing dominates the narrative.

Labor markets remain tight but stable. Unemployment sits at 3.5% at the low end of the recent 3.5–3.6% range, down 10bp over three months and 30bp over twelve months. The Sahm indicator remains benign at 0.07pp. This is a taut but non-accelerating labour market—consistent with wage persistence but not with escalating labour-driven inflation.

Fed assets have rebounded, rising $7B over the past four weeks and $105.8B over thirteen weeks (+2.61%), reversing earlier runoff. This remains $24B shy of the 52-week high, and the expansion is moderate relative to the longer trend. The balance sheet is not contractionary.

Financial conditions have eased materially. The NFCI has risen sharply from -0.62 to -0.43 over four weeks, now at the top of its 12-month range. The curve has steepened: the 2s10s slope now trades at 27bp, up from 12–13bp earlier in the period, recovering from multi-year flats. Both signals point to a loosening of financial conditions and renewed appetite for duration.

The reconciliation turns on whether to treat the hot inflation prints as signal or noise when expectations remain deeply anchored. The labour market is not driving wage acceleration, and the transient nature of recent upside (energy, goods-price passes after a disinflationary period) is evident in the breadth-adjusted read. Expectations have proven resilient at anchor in the face of hot prints before; the recent sharp compression to 1.41% suggests no spillover yet. Real yields have moved substantially lower, pulling down nominal rates and the wedge with it. The widening curve and easing financial conditions reinforce a view that markets are pricing the inflation moment as cyclical, not structural.

arbitrated.notes:
Realized inflation has collapsed sharply off multi-year highs. Headline CPI fell from 2.60% y/y to 0.20% y/y over the last three months (a 2.4pp drop), with month-on-month readings turning deeply negative; core PCE is also down 0.7pp to 1.00%. This is base-effect driven — the 3m annualized headline read of -5.21% shows the magnitude of the disinflationary momentum. But 10-year breakevens have barely budged. They fell 26bp over 63d and 58bp over 252d, but are near the middle of their 12-month range and sit only 85bp below the 2% target. The recent 21d move is essentially flat (+1bp).

This is the signature divergence case: realized inflation hot and collapsing while expectations stay anchored. The expectations read is both fresher and more behaviorally germane to the breakeven wedge. Expectations have resisted downward pressure from the realized disinflation, suggesting either genuine anchoring at target or lag in learning from transitory base effects. Labor tightness data shows the unemployment rate has surged to 13.2% from 3.5% — an almost certainly spurious spike (likely reflecting seasonal adjustment issues or data anomaly), so labor tightness itself is uninformative here. The balance sheet is still expanding (assets +441bp in 4w, +2939bp in 13w), though growth is moderating from the 70% 13w annualized pace. Financial conditions have eased sharply (-36bp 4w) and are now slightly restrictive at -0.21. The curve has flattened somewhat over 21d but steepened significantly over longer horizons.

The break-even should narrow over the horizon, not from a collapsing expectations anchor but from a natural reversion as realized inflation base effects wash through and the gap between print and expectation closes. Realized disinflationary momentum is extreme and unsustainable; base effects from 2024 highs will fade by Q2. Expectations appear correctly anchored. As realized inflation stabilizes at a lower level closer to (but not yet at) the 2% target, the inflation compensation wedge should contract.
arbitrated.falsifier: If core PCE stabilizes above 1.4% and breakevens rise to 1.30%+ while inflation remains below 1%, it would signal expectation upside surprise and flip this read.

risks.text: Fed rate cuts or balance sheet expansion could re-anchor expectations higher than current 1.15% level.
A sharp nominal yield move could mechanically alter the breakeven level independent of inflation expectations drift.
Leveraged funds are heavily short (z=-2.02) and asset managers moderately short; crowding could reverse abruptly on data surprise.
Rolling higher if breakevens widen before mean reversion; carry risk if disinflation narrative breaks.

trade.rationale: Realized inflation is falling dramatically from transitory 2024 highs on base effects. Expectations remain anchored near 1.15%, roughly 85bp below target. As the realized-expectations gap closes from current levels—driven by normalization of base effects rather than expectations de-anchoring—the breakeven wedge should narrow.

why.inflation: Headline CPI collapsed 2.4pp to 0.20% y/y in 3m; 3m annualized is -5.21%. Extreme base-effect momentum is unsustainable and will reverse.
why.inflation_expectations: Breakevens flat 21d, down 58bp 252d, mid-range 12m. Recent stasis despite realized disinflation suggests either true anchoring or lagged learning. No clear signal.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation has fallen sharply from near 2.6% to 0.7%, with the three-month annualized headline declining to -1.59%. Core PCE sits at 1.0%, a full percentage point below target. The recent momentum is weak: headline month-on-month came in at +0.48% but the three-month average is -0.13%, signalling base-effect relief rather than renewed heat. This is deflation by backward-looking measures, a product of the massive 2022 surge rolling off.

Inflation expectations, however, remain remarkably sticky and well-anchored. The 10-year breakeven stands at 1.34%, having risen 47 basis points over three months and 16 basis points in the past three weeks. More critically, it sits at 1.34% against a 12-month high of 1.81% — it is in the upper half of its recent range, not collapsed. This is not an expectations panel in crisis. The Fed's balance sheet has contracted sharply (–15 bp in the past month, –86 bp below its 52-week high), financial conditions have eased substantially, and the 2s10s slope sits at a healthy 50 bp in the middle of its 12-month distribution.

The labour market tells a jarring story: unemployment has surged from 3.5% to 11.0% in the past year, with a Sahm-gap recession signal of 9.5 pp. This is not a labour market story of tightness persisting into inflation — this is a dramatic slackening. The three-month-average unemployment is at 13%, signalling a labour market shock rather than gradual softening.

The reconciliation hinges on the divergence: realised inflation is collapsing due to base effects and labour-market slack, while expectations remain anchored at a level slightly above the Fed's 2% target. The labour read overwhelmingly contradicts any story of persistent wage pressure driving inflation forward. The sticky expectations are better read as anchoring *around* 2%, not as evidence that inflation will not continue to fall as slack widens and base effects dissipate further. Over the one-month horizon, the expectation that realised inflation will continue to fall (on base effects and labour slack) while expectations drift sideways creates downward pressure on the inflation compensation wedge.

The key risk is that a weak labour print may trigger genuine expectations unanchoring — not upward, but downward, if market participants price in a Fed cut cycle. That would narrow breakevens sharply. Conversely, if expectations prove more forward-looking than the current level suggests and begin to price the persistence of slack, they could also compress. The central case is a marginal narrowing of the wedge as realised inflation continues to fall and expectations remain range-bound.

arbitrated.notes:
The 10y breakeven is testing cycle highs after a strong 63-day move (+49bp) and 21-day continuation (+18bp), now at 1.55% and sitting at the 81st percentile of its 12-month range. This elevation in inflation compensation reflects real earnings momentum in headline inflation—the 3-month annualized rate stands at 3.67%, up 68bp over three months, with recent monthly momentum notably positive (0.51% m/m outgoing). Core PCE has also re-accelerated to 1.21% from a 1.00% trough, up 22bp in three months, and now trades 79bp below the 2% target but on an improving trajectory.

However, inflation expectations themselves remain remarkably anchored. The breakeven is near cycle highs in nominal terms, but sits 45bp below the 2% target and only 1.05pp above its 12-month low of 0.50%. The one-year backward-looking move is negative (−23bp), meaning this leg higher has been recent and is not validating a structural shift in expectations. Critically, the 10y breakeven has risen while the Fed's balance sheet has contracted sharply (−60bp in 4 weeks, −3.3% below 52-week highs), and financial conditions have tightened materially (NFCI at −0.46, 13bp below 52-week lows). This is the signature configuration of realised inflation hot while expectations stay anchored—exactly the case where expectations dominate the forward read on the wedge.

Labor market slack has expanded dramatically. Unemployment has risen 6.7pp in three months and now sits 6.2pp above the estimated natural rate, with the Sahm recession indicator at +7.97pp. This loosening, historically a leading disinflationary signal, will likely arrest the recent inflation momentum and suppress expectations of persistent price pressure. The curve has steepened meaningfully over 12 months (+23bp in 2s10s slope), the 2s10s at 0.44pp sits near cycle lows, and both belly and long-end yields have fallen—all consistent with a market that is pricing disinflationary labour dynamics ahead.

The reconciliation is clear: realised inflation has spiked, but expectations have responded by rising only modestly and remain well below target. With labour slack expanding sharply and financial conditions tightening, the near-term inflation momentum is likely to fade. The breakeven's recent rise is a catch-up from depressed levels, not a structural repricing of the inflation wedge. Over the one-month horizon, the most likely path is for inflation surprises to moderate as base effects and the labour slack turn into headwinds, while expectations remain anchored—resulting in a narrowing of the 10y breakeven as realised inflation rolls over and expectations stay put.

{"notes": "The key tension here is between realised inflation picking up and expectations staying anchored—the signature case for a narrowing wedge.

Realised inflation is clearly hot. Headline CPI year-over-year has climbed from 0.20% to 1.39%, a 1.19 percentage point move that puts it at the top half of its 12-month range. Month-on-month momentum is solid at 0.26%–0.28% averaged over three months, well above the low of -0.79% seen earlier. The three-month annualised headline is 4.68%, well above the 2% target. Core PCE has similarly firmed from 1.00% to 1.39% year-over-year, with its three-month annualised reading at 3.26%. The inflation analyst would call this hot.

Inflation expectations, however, show no corresponding lift. The 10-year breakeven sits at 1.63%, essentially flat over the last month (down 0.17pp over 21 days), slightly above its 0.50% 12-month low but still 0.37pp below the 2% target. Over 63 days it has moved only +0.26pp—a gentle rise from mid-2023 lows but nothing that matches the acceleration in actual inflation. The expectations analyst would call this anchored. The range position of 0.87 shows breakevens at the high end of their 12-month band, but that band is narrow (1.30pp), and the absolute level is nowhere near compensating for the realised inflation now running.

Labour is in a sharp cyclical recovery from the pandemic shock. Unemployment has fallen from 14.80% to 7.80% in three months (a 3.20pp drop), though it sits 3.80pp above the estimated natural rate of 4%, so there is slack. The Sahm gap of 5.30pp is elevated, signalling an economy still in recovery mode rather than one with tight labour conditions pushing wage pressure. The labour analyst would see recovery in the data, but not yet tightness in the classical sense. This matters for wage-driven persistence: the labour market is loose enough that we should not expect wage spirals to anchor expectations above where the Fed has credibly signalled them.

Fed balance sheet assets are drifting higher—up 102.7bn in four weeks and 10.9bn over 13 weeks—but the level is 75.8bn below the 52-week high.
