arbitrated.notes:
The key tension here is between realised inflation picking up and expectations staying anchored—the signature case for a narrowing wedge.

Realised inflation is clearly hot. Headline CPI year-over-year has climbed from 0.20% to 1.39%, a 1.19 percentage point move that puts it at the top half of its 12-month range. Month-on-month momentum is solid at 0.26%–0.28% averaged over three months, well above the low of -0.79% seen earlier. The three-month annualised headline is 4.68%, well above the 2% target. Core PCE has similarly firmed from 1.00% to 1.39% year-over-year, with its three-month annualised reading at 3.26%. The inflation analyst would call this hot.

Inflation expectations, however, show no corresponding lift. The 10-year breakeven sits at 1.63%, essentially flat over the last month (down 0.17pp over 21 days), slightly above its 0.50% 12-month low but still 0.37pp below the 2% target. Over 63 days it has moved only +0.26pp—a gentle rise from mid-2023 lows but nothing that matches the acceleration in actual inflation. The expectations analyst would call this anchored. The range position of 0.87 shows breakevens at the high end of their 12-month band, but that band is narrow (1.30pp), and the absolute level is nowhere near compensating for the realised inflation now running.

Labour is in a sharp cyclical recovery from the pandemic shock. Unemployment has fallen from 14.80% to 7.80% in three months (a 3.20pp drop), though it sits 3.80pp above the estimated natural rate of 4%, so there is slack. The Sahm gap of 5.30pp is elevated, signalling an economy still in recovery mode rather than one with tight labour conditions pushing wage pressure. The labour analyst would see recovery in the data, but not yet tightness in the classical sense. This matters for wage-driven persistence: the labour market is loose enough that we should not expect wage spirals to anchor expectations above where the Fed has credibly signalled them.

Fed balance sheet assets are drifting higher—up 102.7bn in four weeks and 10.9bn over 13 weeks—but the level is 75.8bn below the 52-week high. This is not QE-driven expansion; it is the Fed allowing the balance sheet to drift as deposits and currency float. The signal is mildly easing in tone but structurally small.

The curve remains steep at 56bp, near the top of a wide range, and financial conditions are very loose (NFCI at -0.50, well below zero). Risk appetite is sound—copper-gold continues to inch up, the dollar is stable, positioning in asset managers is no longer as short as it was.

Over the next month, the base effect from the CPI printouts earlier in the cycle should continue to fade, but momentum is real. Expectations agents are watching this. The tension is not sustainable: either expectations begin to rise toward realised inflation, or realised inflation comes back down and expectations hold. The panel gives no evidence that expectations agents are racing to catch up. The most likely path is that realised inflation will fade gradually as base effects roll off and the consumption impulse moderates (with looser labour but no wage-spiralling pressure to sustain it), while expectations drift slightly higher from here but remain below realised—a narrowing wedge as the two converge.

More tellingly, the breakeven has traded in a 1.30pp range over the past year (0.50%–1.80%), and currently sits at the 98th percentile of that range—essentially at its 12-month highs. Where they diverge—a hot month or two against a loosening labour market—the expectations analyst holds the informed cross-read here because wage-driven persistence is the mechanism, and wage pressure follows labour tightness with a lag. Labour is now signalling disinflationary momentum ahead. Expectations anchoring against that momentum is the reconciliation: the market is pricing a soft landing after labour reserve has built.

The weighted read is that inflation expectations will begin to narrow as labour disinflationary pressure feeds through realised prints and wage growth moderates. Realised inflation is stirring after months of dormancy. Headline CPI sits at 1.37% (versus 0.20% a year ago), with a three-month annualised rate of 3.69% and recent month-on-month momentum at 0.24%. Core PCE has ticked up more sharply to 1.70% (from 1.00% a year back), and three-month annualised core now reads 2.97%. These moves are not base-effect mirages—core has drifted 0.28pp higher over three months and sits just 0.30pp below target. The labour market remains structurally loose (unemployment at 6.4%, still 2.4pp above estimated natural rate), but has tightened visibly from crisis lows and now sits in the middle of its 12-month range, having fallen 0.50pp in the past three months alone.

Inflation expectations, however, remain eerily flat. The 10-year breakeven has inched to 2.13% after hovering around 2.08-2.10% for months. The move over 21 days is only +0.17pp and over three months just +0.42pp. Critically, the breakeven sits at the absolute top of its 12-month range (1.63pp wide, from 0.50% to 2.13%), with zero room left above. The forward guidance here is not "expectations are rising"—it is "expectations hit their ceiling and have stabilised."

This is the signature divergence: realised inflation hot, expectations anchored, even though anchor itself has tightened to historically tight levels. The curve has steepened sharply (2s10s now at 1.00pp, up 0.80pp over a year), and financial conditions have tightened into -0.62 (near 52-week lows). Fed assets remain elevated and stable. The positioning panel shows asset managers deeply long (+1.14 std devs, up 0.49 from four weeks ago), and levered funds have unwound shorts sharply (-0.40 std devs from +1.10).

Over the horizon ahead, realised inflation is likely to remain elevated but will start to meet base effects and easing comps from a year ago. Expectations have no room to rise further and anchors have proven sticky even as prints climbed. The wedge narrows because realised inflation rolls over from the 3% zone while expectations stay pinned near 2.13%.

A labour market cooling from an elevated baseline supports the expectations-anchoring narrative: wage pressures are likely to ease, supporting the sticky inflation disinflationary trajectory.

The Fed's balance sheet is expanding meaningfully—up $315.5B over 13 weeks and $2.47T over 52 weeks—but is currently at its 52-week high, offering no forward signal of tightening. Curve slope has normalized sharply to 158bp from a 38bp low, compressing the technical cushion for term premium but signalling a return to normal financial conditions consistent with gradual disinflation.

The reconciled read: realised inflation is hot and has surprised to the upside materially, driven by a reversion in monthly prices and possibly base-effect fading. But the expectations framework remains disciplined. Labour markets are cooling from an already-elevated level. The Fed is not tightening. This is the classic disinflationary setup: high realised inflation with anchored expectations means the wedge compresses as realised inflation mean-reverts. Over the one-month horizon to the next CPI, momentum is still upward, but over a 3–6 month horizon, expectations have signalled they do not believe the current realised rate will persist. The 10y breakeven should narrow, not widen.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has surged dramatically, with headline CPI reaching 4.92% y/y and core PCE at 3.54% y/y — both now 1.5+ pp above target. More telling is the momentum: headline is annualizing at 7.49% over three months and mom prints have held above 0.48% for the outgoing period. Core has accelerated similarly to 6.14% annualized. The labor market remains tight with unemployment at 5.8%, only 1.8 pp above natural rate, having fallen 0.4 pp in three months. Both inflation and labor tightness are moving the same direction — higher and tighter respectively — which normally signals persistent upside to inflation pressure.

However, 10y breakevens remain anchored at 2.42%, virtually flat over the past three weeks and only 0.22 pp higher over two months despite headline CPI having jumped 3.25 pp over that same three-month window. The market is pricing inflation compensation 0.42 pp below target, even as realized inflation sits 1.54 pp above it. Breakevens sit in the 91st percentile of their 12-month range, having already moved up from 1.15% lows, but the recent stalling is the key signal. 

The divergence between hot realized inflation and stable expectations is the signature case flagged in the instructions. With headline inflation surging and labor markets tight, market expectations have been tested — and appear to be holding. The flatness of breakevens over recent weeks, even as the monthly CPI print arrived well above consensus, suggests markets are treating the recent pop as either temporary or already fully priced in. This is the expectations read, and it dominates here: inflation compensation should narrow as the three-month momentum moderates toward the baseline and the market realizes inflation is not re-anchoring higher. The Fed's recent moves and forward guidance are likely supporting this expectation-stabilization, and the bond market is ratifying it.

trade.rationale: Breakevens narrowing depends critically on expectations staying anchored as realized inflation moderates from recent highs. Current positioning is crowded long and the three-week flatness is not yet conclusive. Holding flat rather than short avoids duration/policy risk mismatch.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has spiked sharply higher in realised terms, with headline CPI now at 5.25% year-on-year and core PCE at 3.93%, both driven by a material pickup in monthly momentum. The 3-month annualized headline rate sits at 8.17%, well above the 5.70% core annualized, reflecting a temporary goods surge rather than persistent disinflation. However, the critical asymmetry lies in expectations: the 10-year breakeven has barely moved, hovering at 2.40% and below its 12-month high of 2.54%. Over the past three months, breakevens have risen just 8bp despite headline inflation accelerating by 111bp year-on-year. This is the classic "hot realised, anchored expectations" setup.

The labour market shows meaningful tightening: unemployment has fallen 70bp in three months to 5.4%, sitting at the bottom of its 12-month range and only 140bp above estimated natural rate. This tightness will likely sustain the momentum in nominal wages and price-setting behaviour, supporting the inflation persistence case. Yet labour itself is not generating a fresh upside surprise—the jobless rate has simply worked through its cyclical reversion. The Fed's balance sheet has expanded substantially (up 440bn in 13 weeks, 5.66% over the year), providing monetary accommodation that should support demand and price pressure.

The disconnect is telling: realised inflation is hot, labour is tight, monetary conditions are loose, yet inflation expectations remain firmly anchored near 2.4%. This suggests either that the market views the current inflation spike as temporary (goods-driven, base-effect-heavy), or that Fed credibility is holding despite the miss. Given the outgoing 3-month momentum in headline prices (0.37% m/m), near-term inflation prints will likely remain above 4.5%, but expectations are not following. This is the wedge at work. Over the one-month horizon to the next CPI print, expect realised inflation to remain elevated but the expectations read to stay calm unless new persistence evidence (e.g. broader-based wage acceleration or a fresh upside surprise in core services) breaks through. For now, the 10-year breakeven is likely to narrow slightly as markets price the transitory component of the recent spike and the Fed stands firm.

Over the month ahead, expect modest BE narrowing as goods momentum fades and Fed credibility holds, offsetting any near-term inflation print risk.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is hot and accelerating; expectations are cracking under the weight of it, but not fast enough or far enough. Headline CPI sits at 6.90% yoy, up 1.75pp in three months, with near-term momentum elevated (0.86% mom, 9.48% annualized 3m). Core PCE at 4.44% yoy, a smaller but still material +0.51pp in three months, sits 2.44pp above target. This is not a base-effect story: the 3m annualized runs are the centrepiece, and labour tightness remains extreme — unemployment at 4.1%, down 2.6pp in twelve months, with a Sahm gap of only 0.33pp, indicating little slack and strong wage-setting power.

10y breakevens have begun to fall: -0.07pp in 21 days, down to 2.50% from a 12m high of 2.76%. But this fall is shallow relative to the size of realised-inflation overshoot. The breakeven sits only 0.50pp above the 2% target, suggesting markets are pricing in eventual disinflation, but the mismatch between hot realised inflation (6.90% headline, 4.44% core) and a breakeven that has already discounted much of the adjustment is stark. Expectations are anchored relative to the inflation print, not relative to what fundamental economics would suggest: with labour still this tight and momentum this strong, the gap between realised and expected inflation speaks to anchoring power, but it is a fragile anchoring. The curve slope is near the bottom of its 12m range at 0.91pp, and financial conditions have eased significantly (NFCI at -0.57, a 12m high), both of which provide headroom for inflation to persist or re-accelerate if policy loosens prematurely.

The arbitration here is that expectations are holding, but only just. The realised-inflation read is unambiguous: this is hot and broad-based. The expectations read is the limiting factor — breakevens are falling, but shallowly, and from a level that already embedded optimism about path-dependent disinflation. Over the next month, the risk is skewed toward either a stabilisation of expectations if realised inflation moderates, or a re-widening of the breakeven if realised inflation re-accelerates and labour tightness persists. Labour is the binding constraint here: as long as unemployment is this low and momentum is this strong, the case for expectations to re-anchor upward remains live. The preponderance of evidence suggests breakevens widen modestly over the horizon, not narrow further.
arbitrated.falsifier: Unemployment rises more than 0.3pp month-over-month, or core CPI decelerates sharply in the next print, flipping labour persistence and realised momentum assumptions.

risks.text: Curve slope near 12m low (0.91pp); if nominal rates reprice lower on growth concern, breakevens could narrow further despite inflation persistence.
NFCI easing to 12m high (-0.57) may delay policy tightening, allowing inflation to persist longer but also pulling forward any expectations re-anchor.
Breakevens have already fallen 0.07pp 21d; positioning in breakevens is unknown, but recent move may have crowded out continuation risk.
Fed balance sheet at 52w high ($8.68T); QT re-engagement or slowdown would alter the monetary backdrop for expectations.

trade.rationale: Realised inflation remains elevated with tight labour market; expectations are anchored but have fallen sharply and are vulnerable to re-anchoring higher if momentum persists. Modest widening of breakevens over the horizon as reality reasserts itself against the recent expectations correction.

Labor markets remain tight but no longer tightening. The unemployment rate has stabilized at 4.0% after a sharp 2.4pp decline over the past year. The three-month change is now just −0.50pp, a significant deceleration in tightening momentum. The Sahm gap sits at +0.10pp, well below recessionary thresholds. Labor is no longer a driver of worsening inflation persistence.

The divergence is stark: realized inflation hot and rising, expectations stable and low. This is the signature non-persistence signal. Expectations are the binding constraint on future inflation compensation. A static expectations read, especially one that is not even high by historical or target-relative standards, argues strongly for breakevens to narrow rather than widen. The market is pricing 2.4% long-term inflation, the realized rate is 7.5%, and the gap is not being arbitraged by expectations rising. This suggests the market believes the inflation spike is transitory and will revert toward or below trend, anchoring compensation at levels that do not fully compensate for current realized rates.

Financial conditions are loose and stable (NFCI at −0.55, near its 52w high), which supports growth but does not materially alter the inflation-expectations arbitrage. Balance sheet expansion continues (+103k 4w, +304k 13w), providing monetary accommodation but no signal of imminent tightening that would spike expectations.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation remains hot but is showing early signs of stalling. Headline CPI sits at 8.23% y/y with a concerning 3-month annualised rate of 8.80%, though the latest monthly print decelerated sharply to 0.31% m/m from 1.12%. Core PCE is elevated at 5.59% y/y with a 5.48% annualised 3m rate, but the monthly momentum has flattened. The labour market is tight at 3.7% unemployment, only 0.0 pp above its 12-month low, with a tight Sahm gap of 0.07 pp. This tightness supports further near-term inflation pressure.

Inflation expectations, however, are notably anchored and showing no urgency to rise. The 10-year breakeven has traded in a 0.80 pp range over 12 months (2.22% to 3.02%) and sits at 2.88%, only 0.02 pp higher over the past 21 days despite the persistence of high realised inflation. Over 63 days it has risen just 0.44 pp, and the market appears indifferent to the inflation persistence narrative — the range position of 0.82 suggests expectations are elevated but not moving. The breakeven's short-term stasis is the key signal: markets are pricing in that the inflation peak is near and that expectations remain contained around the 2.8–2.9% level.

The critical divergence is clear: realised inflation is sticky but decelerating in momentum, while expectations remain stable and well-anchored despite that stickiness. The curve slope has compressed from +0.39 pp to +0.19 pp over 10 observations, consistent with a market that is not convinced of persistent inflation. Financial conditions have tightened modestly (NFCI at −0.35, near the 52-week high, and at the top of its range), which typically dampens expectations-led expansion. arbitrated.notes:
The panel shows realised inflation cooling modestly while expectations remain sticky, the signature case for favouring the expectations read. Headline CPI has fallen from 8.98% to 8.22% over the trailing three months, and the three-month annualized pace sits at 5.32%, down from 8+ territory. Core PCE has also softened to 5.36% after hitting 5.60% but is still elevated. The monthly prints are volatile—the latest headline mom of +0.06% is benign, but the historical average is +0.43% and the series shows a sawtooth pattern that suggests base effects and energy noise rather than a clean trend. Importantly, core inflation is still 3.36pp above the 2% target, and the three-month annualized core momentum of 5.65% shows inflation persistence has not fully broken.

Against this, the inflation expectations read is notably weak. The 10y breakeven has fallen from 2.62% to 2.48%—a 14bp decline in three weeks, or -17bp over the last nine weeks. The range positioning at 0.27 (well below the 12-month median) and distance of +48bp above target masks the recent softness in the series. Expectations are not anchored; they are drifting down into line with a moderating (but not yet low) realised inflation path.

The labour market remains tight. The unemployment rate is 3.6%, just 0.1pp above the 12-month low, and the Sahm recession rule gap sits at only +0.07pp. This tightness should ordinarily support wage pressure and inflation expectations. However, labour tightness is not actually translating into fresh wage acceleration—the core inflation momentum is stabilizing rather than accelerating, and the three-month change in core expectations is actually flat against a backdrop of stable to slightly loosening headline inflation. The tight labour market is a risk to expectations anchoring, but it is not currently pulling expectations up.

Financial conditions have tightened modestly but remain accommodative (NFCI at -0.24). The curve remains inverted at -30bp, the steepest it has been in recent weeks, though still deeply negative year-to-date. Positioning data shows asset managers have moved from deeply short (-2.01 std devs) to less short (-0.77 std devs), a significant unwinding. Volatility has spiked recently (VIX at 25.56), suggesting some risk-off mood. These shifts do not alter the inflation picture directly, but the moderating financial tightness and the asset manager unwinding suggest some softening in the underlying economic impulse.

The Fed's balance sheet is contracting sharply in the near term (down 38.6bn in four weeks, 62.8bn in thirteen weeks) but this reflects quantitative tightening from a much higher baseline. The pace is less relevant to breakevens than the overall policy stance, which remains restrictive.

Reconciling these reads: realised inflation is cooling but not yet broken, expectations have begun to drift lower, and labour tightness is not yet translating into expectations pressure. The most probable path over the one-month horizon is for expectations to drift lower further as realised inflation continues to moderate, compressing the 10y breakeven. A narrowing of the inflation wedge is the base case. The key falsifier would be a sharp re-acceleration of core inflation or an unexpected wage shock that pulls expectations back up; absent that, the current downward drift in expectations should continue.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation readings show a late-stage disinflationary arc. Headline CPI has rolled over decisively—from 8.98% y/y twelve weeks ago to 7.12% now, placing it at the bottom of its 12-month range. The 3-month annualized headline print at 5.09% sits well below the current level, signalling momentum to the downside. Core PCE is stickier, at 5.46% y/y, but the recent month-on-month print (0.26%) is subdued; the 3-month annualized core of 5.61% reflects elevated prints now aging out, not fresh momentum. Outgoing momentum is weak—the last month-on-month headline was 0.26%—and the forward 3-month average is just 0.42%, down sharply from the 0.69% outgoing print. This pattern is classic base-effect relief driving headline lower faster than underlying disinflation is yet visible.

Breakeven inflation expectations have compressed modestly over the near term. The 10-year breakeven stands at 2.34%, off 17bp in 21 days and 24bp over 63 days. The level sits 34bp above target but remains in the lower half of its 12-month distribution (range width 87bp, position 0.22). The recent weakness is real but not alarming; anchoring appears intact. The market has de-priced some inflation risk in line with the headline roll-over, but has not yet capitulated on expectations. This is the expected response to a late-cycle disinflation where realised inflation falls faster than agents update their long-term views.

Labour tightness has plateaued. The unemployment rate sits at 3.6%, unchanged over three and six months, though down 50bp over the year. The level is 40bp below the estimated natural rate and well above the 12-month low of 3.5%. Wage pressure from labour tightness should persist but faces headwinds from cooling inflation expectations and slowing activity. The labour market is tight but not tightening further; it is stabilising at levels consistent with ongoing but moderating wage growth.

The reconciled read: realised inflation is falling sharply on base effects and momentum, but expectations remain anchored. This is precisely the scenario where breakeven widening stalls or narrows modestly. A steep headline disinflation without corresponding expectations moves narrows the wedge. The market's 17–24bp compression in breakevens over the past 3–21 days reflects this dynamic. Absent a shock to labour-market tightness or a re-acceleration in core momentum, expectations will drift down only slowly over the next month, while realised headline inflation continues to benefit from statistical tailwinds and weak momentum. The net effect is a compression in breakevens toward the low-to-mid 2.2% range.

trade.rationale: Breakevens likely narrow as realised inflation fades on base effects and weak momentum while expectations remain sticky-anchored. arbitrated.notes:
10y breakeven inflation compensation has moved modestly higher over the past month, driven by a realised inflation base that is cooling but unevenly, while expectations themselves anchor but with recent upward momentum. The inflation panel shows headline CPI at 5.96% year-over-year—the 12-month low—with a sharp decline from the 8.98% peak, but the 3-month annualised pace at 3.61% reveals near-trend momentum beneath that favourable base effect. Core PCE at 4.94% is similarly lower in year-over-year terms but the 3-month annualised at 4.55% suggests persistence well above the 2% target. Month-on-month, the most recent print at 0.34% is benign, yet the outgoing momentum was 1.12%, and the 3-month average of 0.30% masks choppiness that includes a recent 0.53% reading.

Against this mixed realised backdrop, 10y breakevens have risen +0.10pp over the past three weeks and +0.11pp over the past nine weeks, moving from a 12-month low of 2.12% to 2.43%, now sitting 34bp above that low and 43bp above the 2% target. The move is small in absolute terms but directionally meaningful given that realised inflation is falling. This suggests expectations are slowly repricing upward even as headline disinflation accelerates.

Labour tightness is flat: unemployment sits at 3.60%, unchanged over the past three months and only 10bp above the 12-month low, with a Sahm gap of just 3bp. This offers no fresh wage-growth signal to explain either inflation persistence or expectations. The labour data neither challenges nor supports the inflation read.

The curve has inverted sharply to -89bp, the steepest inversion in the panel, reflecting two-year yields at 4.81% versus ten-year at 3.92%. This is mechanical—front-end hiking premiums compressing—but it signals that market pricing of near-term policy rates remains elevated, which would normally anchor longer-term expectations if credibility holds. Yet breakevens are nudging higher despite this, suggesting some independence in inflation compensation.

Fed balance-sheet runoff continues at a steady pace: −88bp over four weeks, −239bp over thirteen weeks, on track for −546bp over the full year. This is orderly QT without shock, creating no demand vacuum that would bid inflation premia higher on its own.

The reconciled read is: realised inflation remains sticky above target despite headline disinflation, with core above 4.9% and near-term momentum above trend. Expectations remain anchored to the 2.4% level but are tilting higher at the margin, consistent with a market that sees inflation persistence without conviction that policy will break it quickly. The move in breakevens is modest but consistent with slowly rising inflation term premia as the "last mile" of disinflation proves harder than the headline drop suggests.

Recent 10y move up 40bp in 21 days reflects real yield repricing as much as inflation: inflation wedge may not have widened as much as absolute level suggests.

trade.rationale: Modest long breakeven position: realised inflation is sticky above target despite headline disinflation, and expectations are repricing upward at the margin. Conviction capped by smallness of recent move and staleness risk in expectations measure itself.

Inflation has decelerated sharply into the measurement horizon: headline CPI sits at 4.92% year-over-year, down 1.49pp over three months, while the 3m annualized pace of 4.06% lies firmly below recent highs. Core PCE at 4.78% y/y has softened more gradually (−0.18pp in 3m), but the underlying momentum is moderating—the 3m annualized core pace at 4.74% is cooling. Month-on-month readings have been contained, with headline at 0.31% outgoing and a 3m average of just 0.33%, suggesting base effects are running out and the disinflationary trend is establishing traction.

Expectations present a different picture. The 10y breakeven stands at 2.32%, down 0.16pp over the past three weeks but up 0.05pp over three months and up 0.63pp over the year to date. Critically, expectations remain anchored well below the target of 2.5% (sitting 0.32pp above the Fed's stated 2% goal) despite realized inflation still running 2.78pp above target. The 12m range shows breakevens traded between 2.10% and 3.02%, now in the lower quartile of that distribution. The recent dip in expectations appears technical rather than driven by a collapse in inflation outlook—more a recognition that realized disinflation is working faster than markets feared three months ago.

The key reconciliation: realized inflation falling hard into expectations that remain stable and well-anchored is the textbook signature for breakeven tightening. The gap between where inflation is (4.92% headline) and where markets believe it will settle long-term (2.32% breakeven) is large and growing. As the economy absorbs current disinflation and expectations continue to anchor around the Fed's preferred zone, the inflation compensation embedded in 10y nominal yields should compress. Labour tightness (unemployment flat at 3.5%) remains modest but is not preventing the disinflationary momentum. Financial conditions are easing gently (NFCI at −0.15, moving back to zero from −0.37 lows), which could support near-term growth but does not materially alter the expectations anchoring story.

The Fed's own balance-sheet expansion into month-end (assets +366bp in 4w) is a technical feature of recent banking-stress response and QT pause, not a signal of reflation. Positioning has unwound from 2023 extremes (asset manager z-scores at 0.82 std devs), reducing the risk of a forced unwind narrowing breakevens artificially.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation realised is cooling but with tactical uncertainty. Headline CPI is at 4.95% y/y, down sharply from the 8.98% peak and near the 4.92% twelve-month low; the three-month annualized is now 3.27%, a full 140bp below the year-ago level. Core PCE at 4.78% is sticky but retreating, with core's three-month annualized at 4.74% versus 5.59% a year ago. The most recent month-over-month headline print was 0.34%, but the outgoing print was 0.95%, suggesting some residual momentum risk before the next release.

Inflation expectations, however, have softened considerably and are now anchored well below the realised rate. The ten-year breakeven is at 2.18%, down 16bp in three weeks and 67bp over the past year; it is 88bp above the twelve-month low of 2.10% but sits comfortably within the narrow range. The market is pricing in medium-term inflation well below both current realised rates and the Fed's target, a marked divergence from the persistence signals embedded in wage-sensitive labour tightness.

Labour remains tight but not visibly worsening. The unemployment rate fell to 3.4%, a new twelve-month low, and is 60bp below the natural rate estimate. The Sahm indicator is essentially flat at 10bp, suggesting no imminent labour-market deterioration. Yet with the unemployment rate at its floor of the measured range, wage-pressure transmission risk into core inflation persistence is material even if headline disinflation appears durable.

The curve is inverted at -60bp (2s10s), having recovered slightly from its 252-day range of -1.07pp but remaining deeply negative. Financial conditions have tightened modestly of late (NFCI at -0.18) but remain loose relative to the twelve-month low. The Fed's balance sheet is shrinking on a four-week basis (−143bn) despite a modest thirteen-week gain, reflecting continued runoff.

The reconciliation is this: realised inflation is decelerating on momentum, but expectations are anchored softer than realised rates justify given labour-market tightness. The market has priced in a structural disinflationary regime, a bet that conflicts with wage signals. Over the near horizon to the next CPI release, the momentum read supports disinflationary near-term prints, but the labour tightness–persistence gap creates tail risk to upside inflation-expectation resets if core prints surprise hot. Expectations are not yet vulnerable given their distance from target, but they are vulnerable to a reversal if the labour story reasserts itself and headline disinflation stalls. For now, anchored expectations dominate the signal, but with non-trivial risk to the disinflationary narrative.
arbitrated.falsifier: Core CPI surprise materially hot in next print; labour market re-tightens visibly; Fed balance sheet stabilizes while housing inflation re-accelerates.

Asset manager positioning has reversed sharply higher (+0.94 std dev in 4w); crowded long could trigger volatility on realised disappointment.
Balance sheet runoff is slowing (−143bn 4w but +92bn 13w); if it stabilizes, duration risk reverses and inflation premium may re-price.

trade.rationale: Realised inflation is cooling decisively and expectations are anchored below realised rates, but labour tightness creates material tail risk to upside resets. The near-term momentum supports narrower breakevens but the labour-persistence gap creates asymmetric risk. Positioning as flat pending clarification from next CPI print and labour data.

The configuration is disinflationary: realized inflation is falling fast, expectations are stable and well-anchored, labor is slack without tightening, and the policy backdrop supports disinflation via balance sheet shrinkage and an inverted curve. The task is to judge whether the 10y inflation wedge widens or narrows from here. The risk is that expectations drift lower alongside further disinflation, or that term premium compression narrows the wedge mechanically even if expectations stay put. The median case is a slow grind of realized inflation lower over the next month or two, with expectations either stable or drifting slightly lower, resulting in a modestly narrower wedge as the realized-expectations gap shrinks further. Realised inflation has decelerated sharply from the 8+ percent prints of a year ago to 3.07 percent headline year-over-year, with the 3-month annualised rate at 2.94 percent — nearly at target. Core PCE sits at 4.73 percent, down from 5.6 percent at the cycle peak but still 2.73 percentage points above the Fed's 2 percent target. Month-on-month momentum is subdued at 0.22 percent most recently, with the 3-month average at 0.24 percent. This represents genuine disinflation progress.

By contrast, 10-year breakeven inflation expectations have remained anchored and remarkably stable. The 10y breakeven sits at 2.22 percent, virtually unchanged on the 21-day view (+0.04 pp) and only 0.04 pp below the 12-month midpoint. Over 63 days it is down just 0.10 pp, and the range-position metric places it 23 percent of the way through its 12-month band — demonstrating exceptional stability and near-target anchor.

This is the textbook pattern that should compress the inflation wedge: realised inflation falling away while expectations stay put. The curve slope has inverted substantially (at −106 basis points, the steepest in the 12-month range), and financial conditions have tightened gradually (NFCI at −0.22, near the 12-month low). Fed assets have contracted by 4.19 percent over 13 weeks and 6.41 percent over 52 weeks — quantitative tightening remains active. Labour markets have stabilized but not tightened further: unemployment is at 3.60 percent, up 0.10 pp over three and six months but flat over 12 months, with the Sahm gap at only 0.13 pp.

The narrowing of realized inflation relative to stable expectations should pull the 10y breakeven lower over the near term. Positioning data shows asset managers at historic longs (2.34 std devs) and leveraged funds have just reversed from deep shorts (0.43 std devs), consistent with a market already pricing disinflation but vulnerable to a breakeven compression as the data confirms it. Risk appetite metrics are mixed but not signaling stress that would reverse the disinflationary momentum. The core message is disinflation without expectation destabilisation — this should narrow the wedge.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has cooled sharply from its 2022 peak, with headline CPI falling from 8.22% to 3.72% year-over-year and core PCE declining from 5.61% to 3.83%. The recent 3-month annualized rates—3.67% headline, 2.05% core—suggest momentum has slowed considerably. The last monthly print showed +0.48% m/m headline, elevated but not accelerating. However, near-term disinflation is already locked in by base effects; the more important question for breakevens is whether inflation stabilizes or continues to drift lower.

Inflation expectations (10y breakeven) have compressed sharply over the past year, falling 34 bps to 2.24%. The 21-day change is -12 bps, indicating fresh weakness. Notably, expectations are now only 24 bps above the Fed's 2% target, having spent much of the year in a range of 2.10%–2.59%. The recent downward momentum is clear and material.

Labor tightness has moderated gradually. The unemployment rate stands at 3.7%, up from 3.4% a year ago—a 10 bps shift—but still historically tight. The Sahm rule gap (+0.20 pp) signals some easing, though the rate remains well below the Fed's estimated natural rate of 4%. This suggests labor supply remains a marginal inflation support, but the trajectory is toward normalisation.

The reconciliation hinges on whether the recent pullback in expectations reflects justified disinflation or excessive pessimism. The realised inflation print is cooling, but most of that is base effects. The labour market is loosening only slowly, and core services inflation remains sticky at 3.83%. Crucially, expectations have moved more than realised fundamentals warrant—the 12-month decline in breakevens (-34 bps) far exceeds the narrowing of wage-driven persistence. This suggests market participants are pricing in continued moderation beyond what current labour and core-goods dynamics support.

The immediate risk is that anchor-adjacent expectations are vulnerable to upside surprises in services inflation or sticky wages. But the predominant signal from the panel is that expectations are now *lower* than the underlying inflation momentum justifies, particularly given only gradual labour-market cooling. Breakevens should trade higher over the horizon as markets recalibrate to the stickiness in the core and the lag in labour-market adjustment.

risks.text: If Fed pauses or cuts sooner than expected, expectations may re-anchor lower despite sticky inflation data.
A sharp fall in 10y nominal yields would mechanically narrow breakevens even if inflation expectations widened in isolation.
Asset managers have moved from elevated long positioning (1.48 std devs, down from peak 2.34); a crowd reversal could accelerate expectations downward.
Steepening curve pressure from Fed rate-cut expectations could compress long-end breakevens via carry dynamics.

trade.rationale: Breakeven expectations have compressed excessively relative to realised inflation momentum and the measured pace of labour-market loosening. A reversion toward higher compensation is warranted as services stickiness and labour-market gradualness become clearer.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation itself is in steady disinflation mode, but expectations are not. Realised headline CPI has dropped 0.59pp over the past three months on an annualised basis (3.13% now vs 3.72% three months ago), and core PCE has fallen 0.83pp (3.47% vs 4.30%), both tracking well below the 2.73% and 2.31% annualised 3m rates respectively—evidence of further momentum to the downside. The monthly burn is cooling too: the 3-month average of headline MoM stands at 0.22%, with the outgoing print at just 0.02%, almost 21bps below the recent trend. Core remains 147bps above target, but the trajectory is unambiguous.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, are essentially flat and slightly elevated. The 10y breakeven has drifted down only 19bps over the past three weeks and is essentially unchanged over three months (-3bps) and one year (-2bps). It sits at 2.23%, just 23bps above the 2% target. The market has shown little response to the disinflationary momentum in realised prints. This is the signature case: realised inflation hot (relative to its own recent history, still coming down) while expectations stay anchored. The labour market adds critical context here: unemployment has ticked up modestly (3.70% now vs 3.60% a year ago, though flat over three months), and sits 30bps above estimates of the natural rate, with the Sahm gap at 37bps. The labour market is not acting as a brake on disinflation—it is loosening gradually. This shifts the marginal interpretation of persistence away from wage-push and toward base-effect and service-sector stickiness, both of which are temporary in nature.

The reconciliation is straightforward: realised inflation is disinflating on trajectory, labour is easing, and market expectations for long-run inflation are flat and slightly above target. The wedge (inflation compensation) should narrow as realised inflation continues to drift toward expectations. The 23bp cushion above target in breakevens is not enough to justify widening; it reflects a market that is appropriately (or slightly overly) compensated for the disinflationary path already priced in.

why.inflation_expectations: Breakevens flat over 3m and 1y, unchanged at 2.23%; no fresh signal from expectations panel.

The panel shows inflation cooling into a regime of slower disinflation, while expectations remain anchored but showing early signs of weakness. Headline CPI at 3.09% is down from recent highs but has stabilized; the 3-month annualized rate at 2.63% suggests further gradual disinflation ahead, though the monthly print of +0.31% is meaningfully above the 3-month average of 0.22%, signaling recent upside persistence. Core PCE at 3.16% is similarly steady after sharp recent declines, with the 3-month annualized at 3.29% implying modest residual disinflation but slowing pace. The labour market shows a jobless rate that has drifted higher to 3.7% with a meaningful Sahm gap opening (+0.33pp), suggesting wage pressure is likely easing gradually, which should support disinflation. 

The expectations read is the critical divergence point. The 10y breakeven sits at 2.26%, well-anchored near target and 26bp above the 2% midpoint. Over 63 days it has fallen 18bp; over 252 days it has barely moved (-3bp). The recent 21-day jump of +10bp is notable but sits atop a declining 63-day trend, signaling no meaningful drift in the compensation demanded. Against a panel where realised inflation is slowing and labour slack is emerging, expectations stability to slight softness is the equilibrium read. The financial conditions index at -0.39 is at the 52-week low—tightest conditions in the window—which would normally anchor expectations downward; the Fed's balance sheet is still contracting at pace, compressing liquidity.

There is no cross-read that reframes this. The combination of slowing realised inflation, labour slack opening, tight financial conditions, and stable expectations all point to breakevens narrowing modestly over the horizon as the tail of recent disinflation is priced through and expectations consolidate into a lower band. The recent 10bp bounce in BE is noise atop a structurally gentle downtrend.

The 10-year breakeven has held in a tight 2.30–2.34% range, with the latest observation at 2.33% — up only 7bps over 21 days and 11bps over 63 days, but down 10bps over 252 days. The breakeven sits 33bps above the 2% target but well within normal bounds, positioned in the middle of its 12-month distribution. This is the signature case: realised inflation has sticky floors while expectations remain cool.

Labour tightness is moderating. The unemployment rate has drifted to 3.9%, up 30bps over a year and 20bps over six months, placing it at the top of the 12-month range and 10bps tighter than the estimated natural rate — still tight, but the trend is unmistakably toward loosening. Fed balance sheet contraction continues at a modest clip (−96M over four weeks, −229M over 13 weeks), and financial conditions remain accommodative at −0.42, sitting at their tightest (most accommodative) level in 52 weeks.

The inflation persistence case depends on whether labour loosening persists and continues to relieve wage pressures, allowing core inflation to drift toward target over the next year. The crossread is solid: labour is moving in the right direction for disinflation, expectations are not pricing additional widening, and the policy backdrop remains contractionary in both balance sheet and overnight rates (implicit in positioning and curve slope). The key risk is that sticky core inflation reasserts as labour market resilience persists longer than the unemployment-rate trend suggests, but the expectations anchor appears robust enough to prevent breakeven widening.

Over the one-month horizon, I do not see the drivers that would force inflation compensation to widen. Realised inflation is flatter, expectations are flat to slightly firmer from very anchored levels, and labour tightness is easing. A narrow breakeven — neither widening nor narrowing markedly — is most likely, but the bias tilts slightly toward narrowing as the labour backdrop improves and expectations remain contained.

arbitrated.notes:
The inflation compensation wedge faces crosscurrents. Realised inflation shows two distinct stories: headline momentum has reaccelerated to a 3-month annualised 4.36%, with the most recent monthly print at 0.22% m/m still elevated relative to the outgoing 0.16% baseline, and the 3-month cumulative shift puts headline y/y up 27bp from its 12-month low. Core PCE, however, remains remarkably stable—the 3-month annualised rate of 4.78% masks a core y/y that has drifted only 1bp over three months and sits just 112bp above target. This is the signature divergence: the inflation persistence signal is muddled. Headline is reaccelerating via energy and goods volatility; core is tethered.

Inflation expectations themselves are anchored and range-bound. The 10y breakeven has climbed only 6bp in 21 days and 15bp over 63 days, oscillating in a tight 35bp annual band. It sits 41bp above the 2% target but well below the May 2023 highs. This is precisely the regime where near-term headline noise leaves expectations unmoved. The real test is labour tightness. Unemployment has drifted to 3.9%, rising 20bp in three months but remaining 10bp below estimated natural rate, and the Sahm gap sits at 40bp—still in looseness territory but moving. A labour market that gradually weakens without collapsing would permit core inflation to drift down without expectations re-anchoring upward.

The cross-read: if headline stays volatile but core continues its disinflationary glide, expectations remain the binding constraint on the breakeven wedge. The labour panel suggests slack is returning, not labour-driven persistence. The most likely path is that realised inflation rolls over while expectations remain sticky—that is, the wedge *narrows*, not widens. The current breakeven level already prices in enough slack to do that work.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation has cooled sharply. Headline CPI is at the bottom of its 12-month range (2.97% y/y) after falling 0.52pp over three months, with core PCE at 2.77% y/y down 0.29pp over the same window. Month-on-month momentum is flat (0.20% m/m outgoing, well below the 0.31% three-month average), and the three-month annualized headline print of 0.90% is well below core at 2.81%. This is textbook disinflation—base effects are releasing favorably, and underlying momentum has stalled.

Against this, labor markets are loosening but not dramatically. Unemployment has risen 50bp over 12 months to 4.1%, placing it at the very top of its 12-month range and 10bp above estimated natural rate. The Sahm Rule signals an incipient slowdown (0.47pp gap), but 3-month average unemployment at 3.97% is still tight relative to history. The loosening is real but gradual.

The critical asymmetry: realized inflation is at cyclical lows while expectations remain anchored. The 10-year breakeven is 2.28%, up slightly (−0.08pp over 21 days but +0.08pp over 252 days), sitting 28bp above target and well within its 12-month range (2.14%–2.49%). Expectations have not fallen in step with realized disinflation. This is the signature case outlined in instructions—when realized inflation is hot while expectations stay anchored, resolve toward the expectations driver, not a split. Here the inversion holds: realized inflation is *cool* while expectations remain *sticky on the high side*.

The Fed's balance sheet is contracting steadily (−53M in 4 weeks, −254M in 13 weeks), financial conditions remain accommodative (NFCI at −0.39, near recent lows), and the yield curve is still deeply inverted (−35bp 2s10s). These are conditions that should support long-duration assets and, all else equal, keep inflation expectations bid. Positioning shows asset managers at moderately elevated longs (1.24 std devs) after recent volatility, and leveraged funds have swung from extreme longs to modest shorts (−0.57 std devs).

The reconciliation: realized inflation is disinflationary, labor is loosening, and the Fed is shrinking. But expectations anchoring is holding firm despite the cool prints, and financial conditions remain accommodative. The wedge—10y breakeven inflation compensation—is unlikely to narrow further from here. It may hold or even edge slightly wider as the market waits to see whether this disinflation is durable or a temporary mean reversion after the recent bump. Expectations will only break lower if realizations stay cool *and* the Fed is perceived to have room to cut, or if risk appetite rolls over sharply. For now, the expectations anchor and accommodative backdrop argue for a steady-to-slightly-wider compensation through the horizon.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation is ticking higher in both headline and core measures, with recent momentum visible in monthly prints that have averaged 0.26% m/m over three months against an outgoing 0.19% baseline. The 3-month annualized pace sits at 3.18% for headline and 3.03% for core, both elevated relative to the target 2.5%, and core is currently 99 bps above target. Year-over-year moves show recent uptick: headline has risen 0.11pp over three months to 2.72%, core has risen 0.18pp to 2.99%. These are not dramatic moves, but they reverse the downtrend seen earlier in the cycle.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, remain anchored and have actually softened recently. The 10y breakeven has declined 4 bps over the last 21 days to 2.26%, though it sits 11 bps above the level 63 days ago. The current 2.26% reads 26 bps above the 2.0% target, placing it in the upper half of its 12-month range (2.02%–2.43%), but there is no momentum. The recent decline—from 2.34% eight weeks ago—suggests market participants view the inflation uptick as transient or insufficiently persistent to warrant higher long-term expectations.

Labor markets have loosened visibly. The unemployment rate now sits at 4.20%, up 50 bps over 12 months and 30 bps over the past six months. The 3-month average stands at 4.13%, and the Sahm gap has widened to 43 bps, signaling a material softening. This loosening matters for persistence: a tightening labor market would risk feeding inflation forward, but a loosening one argues against wage acceleration and inflation becoming embedded.

The Fed's balance sheet continues to shrink on schedule. Assets have declined $108M over four weeks and $218M over 13 weeks, with the 52-week contraction reaching $891M. This is mechanical and expected; it removes liquidity but does not signal urgency about inflation control.

The reconciled read: Realised inflation has picked up but remains moderate in absolute terms. Expectations are anchored and softening at the margin. Labor is loosening, which reduces the risk of inflation persistence. The signature divergence here—hot prints but stable expectations—strongly favors the expectations anchor. Over the one-month horizon to the next CPI release, the most likely outcome is that inflation proves sticky but expectations drift sideways to slightly lower as the market remains convinced the uptick is temporary. The 10y breakeven is more likely to narrow than widen.

{"notes": "Inflation momentum has picked up sharply over the last three months—headline is accelerating at a 4.29% annualized pace while month-over-month prints have returned to the 0.40% range after a soft patch. Core PCE has stabilized after falling from 3.01%, now at 2.78%, suggesting some stickiness remaining. The headline-to-core spread has widened again, meaning much of the recent pop is goods-driven and likely transitory, but the 3-month annualized read is the hottest data in the panel and cannot be dismissed.

Against this, 10-year breakevens remain anchored at 2.42%, barely 8bp above where they started the 21-day window and only 12bp above the 63-day entry. The range position shows breakevens near the top of their 12-month band at 93%, yet they have not broken above 2.45% despite headline inflation running at 2.99% year-over-year. This disconnect between hot inflation prints and stable expectations is precisely the signature case for an anchored regime.

The labour market reinforces this story. Unemployment has fallen three months in a row to 4.00% from 4.10%, the tightest reading in the panel, with only a 0-basis-point distance from the natural rate. This is tight by any measure, and wage and demand pressures should be building. Yet the short-term tightness masks a longer story: the unemployment rate is still 30bp higher than one year ago, and the Sahm gap stands at only 20bp, suggesting no recessionary signal yet.

The reconciliation is straightforward: realised inflation is hot and sticky, labour is tight, but inflation expectations have already priced in this regime months ago and are not moving higher on marginal inflation data. The market is saying: inflation is running, wages are tight, growth is okay, but we do not expect to go back to 3.5%+ breakevens or a persistent wage-price spiral. The recent 21-day move of +8bp feels like noise within a stable range rather than the start of a re-anchoring move.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation momentum has picked up sharply over the last three months—headline is accelerating at a 4.29% annualized pace while month-over-month prints have returned to the 0.40% range after a soft patch. Core PCE has stabilized after falling from 3.01%, now at 2.78%, suggesting some stickiness remaining. The headline-to-core spread has widened again, meaning much of the recent pop is goods-driven and likely transitory, but the 3-month annualized read is the hottest data in the panel and cannot be dismissed.

Against this, 10-year breakevens remain anchored at 2.42%, barely 8bp above where they started the 21-day window and only 12bp above the 63-day entry. The range position shows breakevens near the top of their 12-month band at 93%, yet they have not broken above 2.45% despite headline inflation running at 2.99% year-over-year. This disconnect between hot inflation prints and stable expectations is precisely the signature case for an anchored regime.

The labour market reinforces this story. Unemployment has fallen three months in a row to 4.00% from 4.10%, the tightest reading in the panel, with only a 0-basis-point distance from the natural rate. This is tight by any measure, and wage and demand pressures should be building. Yet the short-term tightness masks a longer story: the unemployment rate is still 30bp higher than one year ago, and the Sahm gap stands at only 20bp, suggesting no recessionary signal yet.

The reconciliation is straightforward: realised inflation is hot and sticky, labour is tight, but inflation expectations have already priced in this regime months ago and are not moving higher on marginal inflation data. The market is saying: inflation is running, wages are tight, growth is okay, but we do not expect to go back to 3.5%+ breakevens or a persistent wage-price spiral. The recent 21-day move of +8bp feels like noise within a stable range rather than the start of a re-anchoring move.

Financial conditions have tightened modestly (NFCI at -0.50, range position at 0%), the Fed balance sheet is contracting, and the curve slope has steepened but from very flat levels. None of these readings suggest an environment about to force breakevens much wider.

My read is that breakevens narrow modestly over the horizon, as realised inflation gradually fades from its 4.3% 3m annualized print toward the 2.8-2.9% core run-rate, while expectations stay pinned at 2.40%. This is the market's base case and the data is not forcing a change to it.

arbitrated.notes: Inflation compensation appears anchored despite mixed underlying pressures. The 10y breakeven sits at 2.38%, just 3.8bp above the 2% target, having drifted down 2bp over the past three weeks and remaining in the upper half of its 12-month range (2.02%–2.46%) at 82% percentile. Realised inflation shows a two-tier structure: headline CPI remains elevated at 2.80% year-over-year, with a worrying 4.04% three-month annualised rate underpinned by outgoing month-on-month momentum of 0.44%, but core PCE has decelerated to 2.78%, only 78bp above target. This divergence—hot headline, cooling core—is consistent with base effects and goods volatility rather than persistent wage-driven acceleration. Labour markets are neither tight nor loosening decisively: unemployment at 4.2%, having risen 30bp over the past year and holding at the upper bound of its 12-month range, with a Sahm-rule gap of 20bp. The Fed's balance sheet continues steady runoff (−52b over four weeks, −139b over 13 weeks, −802b over the year), providing modest passive liquidity drain. The 2s10s curve at 25bp is steep by recent standards (63-day change +16bp, 252-day change +66bp) and well-positioned within its range, suggesting some duration expectation is priced. The key tension: realised inflation is front-loaded (headline spiking, but momentum momentum easing), expectations remain well-anchored, and labour supply is gradually firming—the classic setup for mean reversion in inflation expectations toward target rather than de-anchoring. Financial conditions remain accommodative (NFCI at −0.49), and positioning shows modest net short (asset manager z-score at −0.38 after a +0.28 four-week move), suggesting limited crowding to unwind in an upside inflation surprise. Over the next month, the most likely path is a moderate drift lower in headline CPI prints as base effects roll off, reinforcing the expectations anchor. Barring a renewed wage shock or energy spike, 10y breakevens should drift modestly lower.

arbitrated.notes:
Inflation is cooling but has not collapsed, and expectations remain anchored. Realised headline CPI is at a twelve-month low (2.38% yoy), having decelerated 0.49pp over three months; core PCE has fallen 0.32pp over the same window but sits at 2.67% yoy, still 0.67pp above the 2% target. Month-on-month momentum has flattened to 0.22% (the outgoing print), suggesting the downtrend is real but not exceptional. The three-month annualised core rate of 3.49% is still elevated, a signal that base effects are doing the work.

Against this, inflation expectations—the critical read for the breakeven—are extraordinarily well anchored. The ten-year breakeven sits at 2.38%, just 0.4pp above the target and has moved only 4bp over three months and 6bp over a year. It is in the upper half of its 12-month range (0.82 position) but has shown no volatility or drift. The outgoing 21-day change is flat.

Labour is the cross-read that matters here. The unemployment rate has drifted from 3.9% to 4.2% over the past three months—a 30bp rise year-over-year—and the Sahm gap is now 23bp, approaching recessionary warning thresholds. This loosening labour market is consistent with a gradual step-down in wage pressure and inflation dynamics, reinforcing the case that the current disinflation is structural rather than transitory.

The financial conditions index has been tightening (improving, i.e., moving toward less restrictive) very gradually, with NFCI at −0.42 and improving 7bp over four weeks. The Fed's balance sheet continues to contract but at a measured pace (−26bn in four weeks, within normal runoff parameters). The curve slope stands at 34bp, up 66bp over twelve months from deeply inverted territory, suggesting a normalisation rather than a shock.

Taken together: inflation is moderating in a way consistent with expectations remaining anchored and labour slack developing. There is no upside surprise to expectations here, no urgency to shift the inflation compensation priced in. The breakeven should neither widen sharply nor narrow; the current level reflects a reasonable intermediate read where realised inflation is falling toward target while expectations remain stable. The risk lies to the downside if labour continues to loosen and realised inflation accelerates its descent, which could start to pressure expectations downward over the horizon.

Core PCE has rolled over to 2.67% from recent 2.97-2.99% prints. This is genuine disinflationary momentum, especially on the monthly lens: the 3m average month-on-month is just 0.14%, benign.

Yet 10y breakeven inflation expectations have not followed this lower. At 2.23%, they sit 21bp below the 12m high but remain 21bp above the 12m low and have barely moved in 21 days (down only 1.5bp). Over 63 days they are down 17bp, but that trailing move is modest relative to the 67bp fall in headline yoy. The expectations panel shows a range position of 0.48, meaning it is roughly centred in its 12m band, not compressing toward lower anchoring as realised inflation has compressed.

This divergence is the key signal. Labour tightness has eased structurally—unemployment is 4.20%, up 30bp on the year and sitting at the top of its 12m range—which should ease wage persistence. Positioning in longer inflation hedges shows extreme short positioning (asset managers at -2.03 std devs, leveraged funds at +1.21 but after a -0.80 std dev 4w swing, suggesting recent weakness in their shorts). Risk appetite is fragile (vol regime inflated, breadth weak, cyclicals underperforming). 

The reconciliation: realised inflation is rolling over convincingly, and labour is loosening, but expectations have not yet de-anchored to that new reality. The market appears to be pricing in base effects or near-term sticky components offsetting the momentum. However, over a one-month horizon, with inflation prints likely to remain cool, we should expect expectations to follow realised inflation *downward*—the lagged anchor repricing is the dominant signal, not a widening wedge. Confidence is moderate because the positioning (extremely short inflation) and the fragility of risk conditions create tail risks to a sudden widening move, but the base case is for modest narrowing of the wedge as expectations inch lower.

arbitrated.notes:
The 10y inflation breakeven sits at 2.29%, having drifted down 3bp over the past three weeks and 8bp over three months, though it remains 7bp above the 252-day level. The panel shows realised inflation has begun creeping higher: headline CPI is at 2.68%, up 30bp over three months, with the 3m annualized rate at 2.08% — a meaningful acceleration from earlier lows of 2.33%. Core PCE, however, has compressed from its 2.99% peak to 2.78%, suggesting some moderation in underlying price pressures even as headline whips higher.

The critical tension is between these two signals. Realised inflation is lifting, yet expectations remain anchored and have actually softened at the margin. The 10y breakeven's recent weakness — down 8bp in 63 days despite 30bp of headline warmth — reveals that the market is interpreting the pickup as transitory (likely energy and food base effects) rather than a signal of persistent higher inflation. The breakeven is still 27bp above the 12-month low, but positioned in the upper half of its recent range (61st percentile), leaving room to compress if realised inflation disappoints from here or if growth fears drive real yields sharply lower.

Labour tightness offers no fresh signal. The unemployment rate sits at 4.1%, essentially flat over all horizons (3m, 6m, 12m), with the Sahm indicator showing only 20bp of slack. This is consistent with a market that sees wage-driven persistence as contained — not imminent, but not entirely ruled out either. Fed balance sheet contraction continues at a steady pace ($6.66T, down 1.16% in 13 weeks), a mechanical headwind that does not directly drive inflation expectations but reinforces the easing bias in financial conditions (NFCI at −0.49, near its 52-week low).

Curve slope has steepened into recent strength at 52bp, up 14bp in 63 days and 94bp in 252 days. This is typically consistent with growth and inflation optimism, yet the 2s10s is still below its 12-month average. The steepness reflects both a retreat in near-term rate expectations and a market repricing of the terminal rate path — neither is a pure inflation signal.

The reconciliation: realised inflation is hot but expectations are sticky and softening. The market is pricing in transitory pressure, not persistent widening of the breakeven. Over the one-month horizon, headline CPI faces base effects and possible energy softness, while core disinflation should continue to grind. If the market interprets the next print as consistent with this (a warm but decelerating trend), the breakeven should narrow as the recent momentum reverses and growth-sensitive real yields take the bid.

The latest reading is 2.39%, up 10bp over 21 days and 16bp over 63 days, but now sitting 4bp below the 2.43% level from four observations ago. The 12-month range is 2.02%–2.46%, and we are at the 84th percentile — very high — yet the recent trend shows a modest retreat after a July peak of 2.45%. This is the expectations read and it is the one to weight most heavily for a breakeven call.

The realised inflation picture is mixed. Headline CPI year-over-year stands at 2.74%, up 42bp over three months, having recovered from a 2.33% low in September. Core PCE is 2.86%, up 25bp over the same window, but has been range-bound at 2.78%–2.99% for five months. Month-over-month readings are volatile: headline MoM is 0.23% this month after 0.25% previously, but the 3-month annualized is a moderate 2.35% against core at 2.99%. The recent uptick is real but not yet a break higher.

Labour tightness shows unemployment at 4.3%, at the top of the 12-month range (4.0%–4.3%) after rising 30bp over six months. The Sahm gap is +23bp, a warning flag but not yet a recessionary signal. This unwinding of tightness, if sustained, would point toward *lower* wage pressure ahead and *less* inflation persistence — a tailwind for expectations to drift lower. The labour read is improving for the disinflation narrative.

The gap between the two inflation drivers is critical: realised has rebounded, expectations have not broken away. The expectations panel is stationary at the top of its recent range but showing micro-retreat. This is a classic signature case — inflation hot, expectations anchored. The cross-read: labour softening + volatile but modest core momentum + expectations at the ceiling of their normal band = a reading that favours *no net widening* of breakevens over the horizon.

The Fed's balance sheet is in slow contraction (–$4.5B over 4 weeks, –$69B over 13 weeks), and financial conditions remain very accommodative (NFCI at –0.51, at the 12-month low). The curve has flattened 14bp over 63 days to 43bp, but 2s have led the move, not a breakout in real rates. None of this forces a breakeven move; the wedge story is inflation and expectations, not monetary accommodation.

My reconciled read: breakevens are at the top of their range with mixed signals underneath. Expectations are stale at that peak and showing small decay; inflation is elevated but not accelerating; labour is softening. Over the one-month horizon, the odds favour a slight *narrowing* of breakevens as the recent realised-inflation pop fades and expectations remain anchored. This is not a strong conviction — the panel is balanced — but the direction is down for the wedge.

Curve inversion/re-steepening could signal recession fears, pulling inflation expectations down faster than my base case.

trade.rationale: Breakevens are at the 84th percentile of the 12-month range but showing micro-retreat. Realised inflation is rebounding but not accelerating; labour is softening; expectations are stale. Over one month, I expect a modest narrowing of the wedge as the realised pop fades and anchoring holds.

why.inflation: Headline rebounded to 2.74% YoY, but core is flat and MoM momentum is modest at 2.35% 3m annualized. Not accelerating.
why.inflation_expectations: Breakevens at 2.39%, down 4bp in last month, retreating from 2.45% peak. Stale at top of range; micro-decay signal.
why.labor_tightness: Unemployment at 4.3%, top of 12m range, up 30bp over 6m. Sahm gap +23bp. Labour market unwinding supports lower future wage pressure.

arbitrated.notes: Realised inflation shows genuine momentum: headline CPI has moved up 56bp over three months annualized to 2.94%, with month-on-month prints accelerating to 0.35% last month, well above the 0.21% outgoing trend. Core PCE sits at 2.91%, up 13bp over three months, holding stubbornly 91bp above target. This is not base-effect noise—the momentum is broad and sustained. However, the inflation-expectations read reveals a critical divergence. The 10-year breakeven has flatlined over the past month (up only 2bp in three weeks, 7bp in nine weeks) despite this realised-inflation push. At 2.41%, it sits 41bp above the Fed's 2.0% target but is pricing in only modest future inflation. The breakeven remains within its 12-month range (2.02% to 2.46%), positioned at the 89th percentile—near the high, but not breaking out. This is the signature case: hot realised inflation with anchored expectations. When the two diverge this clearly, the expectations measurement dominates the wedge view. The labour market shows no material tightening to explain persistence: the unemployment rate has drifted to 4.30%, at the top of its 12-month range, with a Sahm gap of only 23bp. The Fed has room to stay restrictive without risking imminent labour-driven wage spirals. Financial conditions have tightened modestly (NFCI at -0.52, at its 52-week low), the Fed's balance sheet is shrinking (-39bp over four weeks), and the curve has steepened (+21bp in three weeks), all of which typically compress inflation expectations rather than expand them. The base case is that realised-inflation momentum is temporary or supply-driven, and market pricing of 2.4% inflation compensation already reflects reasonable pessimism. Expectations remain anchored. The breakeven wedge should narrow, not widen.
arbitrated.falsifier: A 15bp+ jump in 10y breakeven on the next inflation print, or unemployment falling below 4.1% with a Sahm gap over 50bp, signalling expectations un-anchor.

risks.text: Asset managers are short-biased (-0.69 std devs), leaving room for positioning unwind if inflation surprises higher again.
Curve has steepened 73bp over 12 months; further steepening could mark a shift in real-yield expectations not captured in breakevens alone.
Fed balance-sheet shrinkage is ongoing; faster or slower QT pace could shift both term premium and expectations simultaneously.
If realised inflation persists beyond three months, expectations will eventually follow, widening the wedge regardless of current anchoring.

trade.rationale: Realised inflation is hot but expectations are anchored. The divergence is the trade. Breakevens should narrow as the inflation momentum is either temporary or already priced in at 2.41%. Labour market is easing, not tightening, removing tail-risk to expectations un-anchoring.

why.inflation: Headline 3m annualized 3.37%, core 2.97%, both rising. Month-on-month prints accelerating to 0.35%. Momentum clear but not yet accompanied by expectations drift.
why.inflation_expectations: 10y breakeven flat (2bp in 21d, 7bp in 63d) at 2.41% despite realised inflation push. Positioned 89th percentile of range, no breakout. Anchored.
why.labor_tightness: Unemployment 4.30% at 12m high, Sahm gap only +23bp. No labour tightening signal. Drift toward ease, not constraint on wage persistence.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is drifting higher in both headline and core measures. Headline CPI y/y stands at 3.02%, near the top of its 12-month range, while the 3-month annualized pace at 3.54% shows momentum. Core PCE at 2.91% is also accelerating—up 0.13pp over three months—and sits 91bp above target. Month-over-month momentum has been consistent, averaging 0.29% m/m and remaining elevated at 0.30% in the most recent print.

In sharp contrast, inflation expectations are completely anchored. The 10y breakeven stands at 2.36%, down 5bp over the past three weeks and clustered tightly in a 2.35–2.38% range over recent weeks. Over 63 days it has gained only 7bp, and it sits merely 36bp above the 2% target—well-anchored relative to the upward drift in realised inflation. The market is pricing almost no response to the hot prints we are seeing.

This divergence is the critical read. Labour markets have loosened noticeably—the unemployment rate has risen 30bp over 12 months and sits at 4.40%, at the top of its 12-month range with a positive 33bp Sahm gap signal—which should support moderating wage pressure and inflation drift lower over the medium term. However, the near-term realised inflation momentum is real and persistent, driven by a combination of base effects unwinding slowly and underlying demand still outpacing supply slightly.

The disconnect between hot current inflation and unmoved expectations reflects either confidence that this is transitory, or—more likely—that market participants see the labour-market loosening as a genuine disinflationary force sufficient to pull expectations down if inflation proves sticky. The Fed's recent balance sheet normalization (down 54bn over 13 weeks, 472bn over 52 weeks) is also contributing to tighter conditions in the background.

Given the stale expectations read and the strong cross-signal from improving labour tightness, I weigh the expectations panel most heavily here. Expectations are anchored and resisting upward pressure from current prints—a sign of genuine credibility. Breakevens should remain range-bound to slightly wider, since some of the realised inflation momentum is real, but the anchor is holding.

arbitrated.notes:
Realised inflation is running hot, with headline momentum still elevated at 0.29% m/m (equal to the 3m average) and 3m annualised headline at 3.54%. However, this is mixing a recent softening in the monthly data trend—headline CPI y/y has come down 6bp in the last month and core has fallen 8bp—against a still-firm underlying picture. Core PCE at 2.75% remains 75bp above target. The momentum is concerning but the deceleration signal is real.

Inflation expectations, by contrast, show striking stability and anchoring. The 10y breakeven sits at 2.30%, well-contained within its 12m range of 2.17–2.46%, positioned at the midpoint (0.45 range position). Changes are minimal: -5bp over 21d, -3bp over 63d, +1bp over 252d. This is the signature case the framework warns against: realised inflation hot while expectations stay anchored. Under that read, the expectations driver dominates the wedge direction.

Labour tightness is loosening visibly. The unemployment rate has risen 30bp over 12m and 33bp over 3m, now at 4.40% (the high end of its 12m range). The Sahm gap stands at +0.33pp, signalling recession-adjacent slack. This rising unemployment materially reduces medium-term inflation persistence risk and supports the expectations-anchoring story.

The Fed's balance sheet continues a steady shrink: -55.5bn over 13w, -426bn over 52w. This is neither stabilising nor re-expanding, just gradual runoff. The curve has steepened modestly (+35bp over 252d) and sits at the upper end of its 12m range (0.75 range position), reflecting both short-end rate expectations and a benign term premium backdrop.

Taken together: realised inflation is moderating from recent highs, labour is loosening (reducing persistence risk), and expectations are rock-solid anchored. The wedge should narrow because the near-term realised overshoot is dissipating into a stable, target-consistent expectations regime. This is mean reversion in the inflation compensation, not a break in credibility.

arbitrated.notes: Realised inflation is hot but narrowing, expectations are anchored and drifting lower. Headline CPI sits at 2.99% year-over-year, near the top of its 12-month range (2.33–3.02%), but the three-month annualized headline prints at 3.64%—significantly elevated. Critically, this realised warmth is not translating to higher inflation compensation. Labour tightness is easing sharply—unemployment has risen 0.40pp over 12 months to 4.50%, now at the top of its range, and the Sahm gap signals recession risk at +0.40pp. The combination of softening wage pressure and expectations that remain well-anchored despite the headline bump points to base effects and transitory components driving the recent inflation print, not persistent demand.
